title: Viruses and the edge of life: can one definition sort the living from the non-living?

summary.text: A virus can copy itself, yet it is not a cell, so is it alive? In this lesson you will play a copying game to see how mistakes build up, test 20 cases against NASA's definition of life, and walk a scale to find out how small a virus is.
summary.art: A small spiky virus particle resting on a brass door handle, beside a cut-away view of a nose cell crowded with new copies of the same virus.

intro.hook: Doctors say that soap 'inactivates' a cold virus. Many of them avoid the word 'kills'. Can you kill something if nobody agrees that it is alive?
intro.text: A teaspoon of sea water from Marina Beach in Chennai holds about fifty million viruses. Almost none of them can harm you. Nearly all of them infect the bacteria of the sea. A virus is a set of instructions wrapped in a coat. Alone, a virus particle takes in nothing and makes nothing. Inside the right cell, the cell reads the instructions and builds more viruses. So the same virus looks like a speck of dust in one place and like a living being in another. In this lesson you will find out why scientists cannot agree about viruses, what NASA means by the word 'life', and whether life on another world might be built in a different way.
intro.art: A child holding a teaspoon of sea water up to the light on a beach, with a magnified circle showing many tiny virus particles among a few larger bacteria.

outcomes: I can say what a virus is made of, and what a cell has that a virus lacks.
I can describe, step by step, how a cell copies a virus.
I can explain why viruses evolve, using copying, mistakes and selection.
I can state NASA's working definition of life and explain its three parts.
I can give reasons for and against calling a virus alive.
I can explain why a definition of life is a tool, and name cases that strain it.
I can describe how life on another world might differ, and what it would still need.
I can plan a fair test, predict with a reason, and say what my results show.

terms.meaning: A virus is a set of instructions, called a genome, wrapped in a coat of protein. A virus can be copied only inside a living cell.
terms.example: The virus that causes a common cold is copied inside the cells that line your nose.
terms.art: A small round particle with a coiled thread inside and a coat made of many identical small pieces.

terms.meaning: A virion is one complete virus particle outside a cell. It is the form in which a virus travels from one cell to the next.
terms.example: A sneeze carries thousands of virions in tiny drops of water.
terms.art: A single virus particle floating inside a tiny drop of water in the air.

terms.meaning: A genome is the full set of instructions for building a living being or a virus. It is written as a long chain of chemical letters.
terms.example: Your genome has about 3,000 million letters. The genome of a flu virus has about 13,500.
terms.art: A very long ribbon of four repeating colours beside a very short ribbon of the same four colours.

terms.meaning: DNA and RNA are the two chemicals that genomes are written in. Each is a long chain made of four kinds of small units, which we call letters.
terms.example: Your genome is DNA. The genomes of the flu virus and the measles virus are RNA.
terms.art: A twisted ladder labelled DNA beside a single wavy strand labelled RNA, each built from four colours of beads.

terms.meaning: A protein is a chain of small units called amino acids, folded into a shape that does a job. Cells build proteins by reading genes.
terms.example: The coat of a virus is made of proteins. So are your muscles and the keratin of your nails.
terms.art: A string of coloured beads folding up into a compact, knobbly shape.

terms.meaning: A capsid is the protein coat of a virus. It is built from many copies of the same few proteins, and it protects the genome inside.
terms.example: The capsid of tobacco mosaic virus is a hollow rod made of 2,130 copies of one protein.
terms.art: A hollow rod built from identical small blocks arranged in a spiral, with a thread running inside.

terms.meaning: An envelope is a thin layer of fat that some viruses carry outside their capsid. The virus takes it from the membrane of the cell that made them.
terms.example: Flu viruses and measles viruses have an envelope. Polio viruses do not.
terms.art: A virus capsid wrapped in a thin soft outer layer studded with small spikes.

terms.meaning: A host cell is a living cell that a virus gets into and that then builds new viruses.
terms.example: For tobacco mosaic virus, the host cells are the leaf cells of tomato, tobacco and chilli plants.
terms.art: A large plant cell with a few small rod-shaped virus particles inside.

terms.meaning: A receptor is a molecule on the outside of a cell that has a job for the cell. A virus can enter only a cell whose receptor fits the virus's coat, as a lock fits a key.
terms.example: The measles virus fits a receptor found on human cells, so measles spreads only among humans.
terms.art: A key-shaped spike on a virus fitting into a matching notch on the surface of a cell.

terms.meaning: A ribosome is a tiny machine inside a cell that reads instructions and joins amino acids into proteins. Every cell has ribosomes. No virus has them.
terms.example: One bacterium holds thousands of ribosomes. They build virus proteins when a virus's instructions arrive.
terms.art: A small two-part blob with a ribbon passing through it and a chain of beads growing out of the top.

terms.meaning: A mutation is a change in a genome. Most mutations are copying mistakes, where one letter is swapped, lost or added.
terms.example: Flu viruses pick up mutations every year, which is why last year's flu vaccine may not fit this year's virus.
terms.art: Two rows of coloured letters that match everywhere except one letter, which is circled.

terms.meaning: Darwinian evolution is change over generations that happens when copies differ a little, the differences are passed on, and some copies leave more copies than others.
terms.example: A virus with a mutation that helps them enter cells leaves more copies, so that mutation becomes common.
terms.art: Five rows of small shapes, where one slightly different shape becomes more and more common from the top row to the bottom.

terms.meaning: Self-sustaining means keeping yourself going. A self-sustaining system takes in energy and materials and uses them to build and repair its own parts.
terms.example: A curd bacterium takes in milk sugar and builds new parts from it. A virus particle on a spoon does not.
terms.art: A bacterium with arrows showing sugar going in and new parts being built inside.

terms.meaning: A working definition is a rule that people agree to use for now, because it is useful. They expect to change it when they learn more.
terms.example: NASA's definition of life is a working definition, written to guide the search for life on other worlds.
terms.art: A notebook page with a sentence written in pencil and an eraser lying beside it.

terms.meaning: A bacteriophage, or phage, is a virus whose host cells are bacteria. Phages are the most common viruses on Earth.
terms.example: The phage called T4 infects the gut bacterium E. coli and looks like a tiny moon lander.
terms.art: A virus with an angular head, a straight tail and thin legs standing on the surface of a rod-shaped bacterium.

terms.meaning: A giant virus is a virus as large as a small bacterium, with hundreds or thousands of genes.
terms.example: Mimivirus has about 1,000 genes. A flu virus has about 12.
terms.art: A large many-sided virus particle covered in fine fibres, drawn beside a much smaller flu virus for size.

terms.meaning: A viroid is a short loop of RNA with no coat at all. A viroid carries no instructions for any protein, yet plant cells make copies of them.
terms.example: A viroid of only 246 letters killed millions of coconut palms in the Philippines.
terms.art: A tiny closed loop of thread, drawn beside a much larger virus particle.

terms.meaning: To inactivate a virus is to damage them so that no cell can copy them any more.
terms.example: Soap inactivates a flu virus by pulling apart the envelope of fat around them.
terms.art: A virus particle whose outer layer is peeling away in a patch of soap bubbles.

terms.meaning: A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Scientists measure viruses in nanometres.
terms.example: A flu virus is about 100 nanometres across. Ten thousand of them in a row would cross one millimetre.
terms.art: A ruler's one-millimetre mark magnified again and again until a row of tiny virus particles can be seen.

terms.meaning: Astrobiology is the science that studies how life begins, and whether there is life beyond Earth.
terms.example: Astrobiologists study the hot springs of Puga valley in Ladakh to learn how life copes with harsh places.
terms.art: A scientist in a warm jacket taking a water sample from a steaming hot spring in a bare mountain valley.

explanations.concept: What a virus is made of
explanations.definition: A virus is a genome of DNA or RNA inside a coat of protein called a capsid. Some viruses also have an outer envelope of fat.
explanations.description: A virus has very few parts. In the middle is the genome, a chain of chemical letters that holds the instructions. Around the genome is the capsid, a coat built from many copies of the same few proteins. Why so few kinds of protein? A genome this short has room for only a few instructions, so one small protein is made again and again and stacked into a shell. Some viruses, such as flu and measles, also wear an envelope. This is a thin layer of fat that the virus takes from the membrane of the cell that built them. Viruses are very small. Most are between 20 and 300 nanometres across, and a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. A light microscope cannot show a thing that small, because the waves of light are wider than most viruses. So scientists use an electron microscope, which uses a beam of electrons in place of light.
examples: Tobacco mosaic virus is a stiff rod 300 nanometres long. It has one strand of RNA with about 6,400 letters, inside 2,130 copies of one coat protein.
A flu virus has 8 short pieces of RNA, about 13,500 letters in all, inside an envelope with spikes.
In 1964 June Almeida, a Scottish scientist who had left school at 16, took the first electron microscope pictures of a human coronavirus.
explanations.art: A cut-away virus particle showing three labelled layers: a coiled genome in the middle, a capsid of repeating blocks, and an outer envelope with spikes.
explanations.context: This card explains the parts of a virus: the genome, the capsid and, in some viruses, an envelope.

explanations.concept: What a cell has that a virus particle does not
explanations.definition: A cell has ribosomes to build proteins and a way to get energy from food or light. A virus particle has neither.
explanations.description: Compare a virus with the smallest living cell. A cell has a membrane that takes in food and keeps the inside different from the outside. A cell has thousands of ribosomes, the machines that read instructions and build proteins. A cell breaks down food to get energy, and stores that energy in a small molecule called ATP. With these, a cell builds every part of a new cell. A virus particle has instructions and a coat, and usually nothing else. They have no ribosomes, so they cannot build a single protein. They make no ATP, so they have no supply of energy. This is why a virus particle outside a cell takes in nothing and builds nothing. It is also why antibiotics do not cure a cold. An antibiotic works by jamming a part that bacteria have, such as the bacterial ribosome or the bacterial cell wall. A virus has no such part to jam.
examples: A curd bacterium in warm milk takes in milk sugar and divides about once an hour. A virus particle in the same milk stays just as they are.
Scientists can grow bacteria in a dish of broth. Nobody has ever grown a virus in broth without living cells in it.
Flu viruses for vaccines are grown inside fertilised hens' eggs, because the viruses need living cells.

Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, who was born in Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, helped to map the ribosome atom by atom. The maps show where antibiotics jam the bacterial ribosome. He shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009.
explanations.art: A bacterium with a labelled membrane, ribosomes and an energy symbol, beside a virus particle with only a genome and a coat labelled.
explanations.context: This card compares a virus particle with a living cell, part by part.

explanations.concept: How a cell copies a virus
explanations.definition: A virus is copied in six steps: attach, enter, uncoat, copy and build, assemble, and leave.
explanations.description: First the virus particle bumps into a cell by chance. If a protein on the virus's coat fits a receptor on the cell, the two stick together. This is the attach step. A receptor is there for the cell's own use, for example to take in food or to receive signals. The virus fits it the way a copied key fits a lock. Second, the virus or their genome gets inside. Third, the coat comes off and the genome is free. Fourth, the cell's ribosomes read the virus's genome in the same way as the cell's own genes, and build virus proteins. The cell also copies the virus genome many times. Fifth, the new coat proteins and the new genomes join up into new particles. In many viruses they do this by themselves, because their shapes and electric charges fit together. Sixth, the new particles leave. Some burst the cell open, and some bud out through the membrane and take a piece of it as an envelope. The fit between coat and receptor explains why each virus has only certain hosts. A virus whose key fits no lock on your cells cannot infect you.
examples: A T4 phage lands on a bacterium, injects their DNA, and about 25 minutes later 100 to 200 new phages burst out.
Tomato mosaic virus has no way through a plant's cell wall. They enter through a tiny wound, such as a broken leaf hair.
You can eat a tomato from a plant with mosaic virus. Your cells have no receptor that fits this virus.
explanations.art: Six small numbered pictures in a circle around a cell: a virus attaching, entering, shedding the coat, being copied, new particles forming, and the particles leaving.
explanations.context: This card explains the six steps by which a cell copies a virus, and why each virus has only certain hosts.

explanations.concept: Why viruses evolve, and why some evolve fast
explanations.definition: Viruses evolve because their genomes are copied with small mistakes, the mistakes are passed on, and some copies get into more cells than others.
explanations.description: Evolution needs three things. There must be copies. The copies must differ a little, and the differences must be passed on. And some copies must leave more copies than others. Viruses have all three. When a cell copies a virus genome, the copying enzyme sometimes puts in a wrong letter. A copying enzyme is a protein that builds the new chain, one letter at a time. Your own cells check each new letter and repair most mistakes, so only about one letter in a thousand million ends up wrong. Most RNA viruses bring a copying enzyme that does no checking. It gets about one letter wrong in every ten thousand to hundred thousand. One infected cell makes thousands of copies, so many of the new viruses differ from the parent by a letter or two. Most changes do harm, and those viruses are not copied again. A few changes help, for example by hiding the virus from the body's defences. Those viruses are copied more, and soon they are the common kind. Nothing in this needs the virus particle to do any work. The cell does the copying, and the world does the choosing.
examples: Flu viruses change enough each year that a new flu vaccine is made for most years.
During the Covid-19 pandemic, scientists read millions of virus genomes and watched new variants appear and spread.
Coronaviruses have an unusual checking enzyme. It lets them keep a genome of 30,000 letters, which is very long for an RNA virus.
explanations.art: A row of virus genomes drawn as strips of letters, each with one or two changed letters, and one changed strip that becomes common in the row below.
explanations.context: This card explains why viruses change over the years, using the three things that evolution needs.

explanations.concept: NASA's working definition of life, word by word
explanations.description: In 1994, a group of scientists advising NASA needed a definition to guide the search for life on other worlds. They agreed on this one: 'Life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution.' The biochemist Gerald Joyce wrote it down, and he says that Carl Sagan suggested the idea. Take it one part at a time. 'Chemical system' means a group of chemicals that act on one another. This leaves out computer programs, which are patterns in a machine. 'Self-sustaining' means the system keeps itself going. It takes in energy and materials and builds its own parts. 'Capable of Darwinian evolution' means it makes copies that differ a little and pass the differences on, so that its kind can change over generations. Why these three? A flame is chemical and keeps itself going, but it has no instructions to pass on, so a flame fails the third part. A virus is chemical and evolves, but a virus particle builds nothing by themselves, so a virus fails the second part. Of all the things we know, only cells pass all three. The definition has problems. A mule cannot have young, so one mule cannot evolve. The definition must be about a kind of being over many generations, and that makes it hard to use on one sample from Mars. And no living thing is fully self-sustaining. You cannot make your own food, and you need plants to do it. So 'self-sustaining' is a matter of degree.
examples: A candle flame: chemical, keeps itself going while the wax lasts, but cannot evolve. Two parts out of three.
A cold virus on a door handle: chemical, their kind evolves, but they do not keep themselves going. Two parts out of three.
A curd bacterium: chemical, self-sustaining and able to evolve. Three parts out of three.

perspectives.who: Gerald Joyce and the NASA group, 1994
perspectives.explanation: The definition is a useful guide for now. Evolution is the one thing that life does and that nothing else in chemistry does, so a test for life should look for it.

perspectives.who: Carol Cleland, a philosopher of science
perspectives.explanation: It is too early to define life. We know only one kind, the life of Earth, and all of it is related. A definition made from one example may describe only that example.
A probe cannot wait for generations to watch evolution. It needs signs it can measure in a day, such as molecules too complicated to form without life.

explanations.art: The sentence 'Life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution' written on a board, with its three parts underlined in three colours.
explanations.context: This card takes NASA's definition of life apart, one part at a time, and shows where it runs into trouble.

explanations.concept: The great debate: is a virus alive?
explanations.description: Scientists agree about what a virus is made of and what a virus does. They disagree about which word fits. The disagreement is not about facts. It is about which test for life matters most. If you think life means doing your own chemistry, a virus fails. If you think life means carrying instructions that evolve, a virus passes. A third group points out that we may be looking at the wrong object. A seed in a jar and the plant in the field are the same being at two stages. Perhaps the virus particle is like the seed, and the infected cell is the virus's active stage. You can test each view against the hard cases in this lesson. Ask which cases the view sorts well, and which ones it sorts oddly.
examples: A doctor says a vaccine holds 'live virus' or 'killed virus'. She is using the words of life.
A chemist can store tobacco mosaic virus as crystals in a bottle. She is treating the virus as a chemical.
Both of them are describing the same particle correctly.

perspectives.explanation: Viruses are not alive. They have no chemistry of their own and they do not copy themselves, because cells copy them. Many of their genes were taken from their hosts. Life is made of cells, and viruses are something cells produce.

Viruses are alive, but the particle is only their travelling stage. The living stage is the infected cell, which he calls a virocell. A virocell takes in food, makes energy and builds, all under the virus's instructions.

'Alive' has no sharp edge. Stones, prions, viroids, viruses, bacteria that live only inside other cells, and free-living bacteria form a long slope. It is more useful to say what each one can do than to argue about one word.

explanations.art: One virus particle in the middle of the page with three speech bubbles around it, reading 'a chemical', 'alive when inside a cell' and 'the word has no sharp edge'.
explanations.context: This card sets out the three main answers scientists give to the question 'Is a virus alive?'

explanations.concept: Giant viruses, tiny cells, viroids and prions: the cases in between
explanations.definition: Between a stone and a free-living cell there are many kinds of things: prions, viroids, small viruses, giant viruses, and cells that can live only inside other cells.
explanations.description: For a long time, the rule seemed simple. Viruses were tiny and had a handful of genes, and cells were big and had thousands. Then the gap began to fill from both sides. In 1992, a microbe was found in a water cooling tower in Bradford in England. The microbe was large enough to see with a light microscope, so scientists filed them as a bacterium. In 2003, Bernard La Scola and his team in France showed that the microbe was a virus, and gave them the name mimivirus. Mimivirus has about 1,000 genes, more than some bacteria have. A few of those genes are for parts of the protein-building system, which no virus was supposed to have. Mimivirus still has no ribosomes, so the virus still needs a cell. In 2008, the same team found a small virus, Sputnik, that can be copied only inside the copying factory of a giant virus. From the other side, scientists found bacteria that have lost most of their genes. Carsonella lives inside the cells of a plant-sucking insect and has only 182 genes. Carsonella cannot live outside those cells, yet every biologist calls them a living cell. Below the viruses there are simpler things still. A viroid is a bare loop of RNA, a few hundred letters long, with no coat. A prion is a wrongly folded protein that makes normal proteins of the same kind fold wrongly too. A prion has no genome at all, yet prions spread.
examples: Mimivirus: about 1,000 genes, no ribosomes, copied only inside an amoeba.
Carsonella: 182 genes, has ribosomes, lives only inside insect cells.
Potato spindle tuber viroid: 359 letters of RNA, no coat, no protein, found by Theodor Diener in 1971.
explanations.art: A long slope with seven things placed along it from left to right: a stone, a prion, a viroid, a small virus, a giant virus, a tiny bacterium inside another cell, and a free-living bacterium.
explanations.context: This card is about the things that sit between viruses and cells, and below viruses, which make a sharp line hard to draw.

explanations.description: Some phages do not burst their host cell straight away. They can slip their genome into the bacterium's own genome and wait there, and they are copied each time the bacterium divides. So each phage has two paths: burst out now, or hide and wait. In 2017, a team led by Rotem Sorek in Israel found how one group of phages chooses. Each time one of these phages infects a bacterium, the infected cell lets out a small signal molecule. The team named it arbitrium, from the Latin word for decision. Later phages measure how much arbitrium is around. If there is a lot, many bacteria have already been infected and few hosts are left. Then the phage hides and waits. If there is little, the phage bursts out. So these viruses send a signal, read it and act on it. Bacteria respond too. Many bacteria keep short pieces of the DNA of phages that attacked them, in a part of their genome called CRISPR. With these pieces they recognise the same phage later and cut that phage's DNA.
examples: A phage that finds few hosts left hides in the bacterium's genome and waits for better times.
A bacterium who survives a phage keeps a piece of that phage's DNA and passes the piece on to their daughter cells.
Scientists turned CRISPR into a tool for editing genes. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 2020.

perspectives.explanation: These phages sense a signal, compare its amount and take one of two paths. That is sensing, deciding and acting, done with a few molecules. Viruses think in this simple way, as cells do.
These are chemical switches. A molecule binds a protein, and the protein turns a gene on or off. They would rather not use the word 'decide', because nobody has shown any awareness behind it.

explanations.art: Phages around a group of bacteria with small dots of signal drifting between them, and one phage curled up asleep inside a bacterium's genome.
explanations.context: This card is about viruses that send and read signals, and about bacteria that keep a record of the viruses they have met.

explanations.description: Nobody knows where viruses came from. Viruses leave no fossils, and their genomes change so fast that old traces are wiped out. There are three main ideas. All three may be true for different viruses. What scientists do agree on is that viruses are very old. Viruses infect every branch of cellular life, and some virus coat proteins have the same folded shape in viruses of bacteria and viruses of humans. That points to viruses that already existed when the first cells were alive, more than 3,000 million years ago.
examples: A coat protein with the same fold is found in a phage of bacteria and in a virus of humans, which suggests one very old ancestor.
Mimivirus has genes for protein-building, which could be leftovers from a cell ancestor or could have been picked up from hosts.
Some genes in cells can jump from place to place in the genome. A jumping gene that gained a coat would look much like a virus.

perspectives.explanation: Viruses began as pieces of a cell's genome that gained a coat and became able to move from cell to cell.
Viruses began as small cells that lived inside larger cells. Over a very long time they lost every part they could borrow from the host, as Carsonella is doing now.

perspectives.who: The virus-first idea, argued by Eugene Koonin and others
perspectives.explanation: Things like viruses were copying themselves before the first true cells existed. On this view, viruses did not come from cells. They are as old as life, or older.

explanations.art: Three small picture-stories side by side: a piece of genome leaving a cell in a coat, a small cell shrinking inside a big one, and loose strands being copied in an ancient pool.
explanations.context: This card gives the three main ideas about where viruses came from. Nobody knows which is right.

explanations.concept: What viruses do in the living world
explanations.definition: Viruses are the most numerous biological things on Earth. They recycle nutrients in the sea, move genes between living beings, and have left their genes in every genome, including yours.
explanations.description: Most people meet viruses only as illness. That is a small part of what viruses do. A millilitre of surface sea water holds about ten million virus particles. Almost all of them are phages, whose hosts are bacteria. Every day, viruses, mostly phages, kill about a fifth of all the tiny living things in the sea. Most of these are bacteria. The burst cells spill their contents into the water, and other microbes feed on them. So viruses keep carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus moving through the sea. Viruses also carry genes from one host to another. And sometimes a virus genome gets stuck in the genome of an egg or sperm cell, and is passed to every descendant. About 8 of every 100 letters in the human genome came from such viruses. Some of those old virus genes now do jobs for us. A gene called syncytin once made the envelope protein of a virus. Today it builds a layer of the placenta, the organ that feeds a baby before birth. The placenta as we know it could not form without that old virus gene.
examples: There are thought to be about ten times as many viruses in the sea as bacteria.
In 1896, Ernest Hankin reported that water from the Ganga and the Yamuna destroyed cholera bacteria, even after filtering. Phages are one possible cause, and scientists still debate it.
Indian farmers spray a virus called HaNPV on chickpea and cotton. The virus infects only the caterpillars of the pod borer moth.
explanations.art: A sea scene in cross-section with bacteria bursting open in the water, tiny phages drifting out, and small arrows showing nutrients passing to other microbes.
explanations.context: This card is about what viruses do in the sea, on farms and in our own genomes, apart from causing illness.

explanations.concept: Life as we do not know it: what could be different on another world?
explanations.description: All life on Earth is related, so we have only one example of life. It uses water as its liquid, carbon chains as its frame, and DNA or RNA for its instructions. Which of these are needed, and which are only how things happened here? Start with the liquid. Chemicals must meet in order to react, and they meet easily when they are dissolved in a liquid. Water is very good at dissolving salts, sugars and many other chemicals. Titan, a moon of Saturn, has lakes of liquid methane and ethane at about 179 degrees below zero. These are oily liquids. Salt and sugar do not dissolve in them, and neither does DNA. Life in such a lake would need different molecules and a different kind of membrane. Next, the frame. A carbon atom makes four bonds, so carbon atoms join into long chains and rings. Silicon also makes four bonds, but chains of silicon atoms break apart in water, and silicon joined with oxygen becomes solid rock. So most scientists think carbon is the likelier frame. Last, the instructions. In 2012, a team led by Philipp Holliger in Cambridge built six new chemicals, called XNAs, that can store instructions and be copied with changes. So DNA and RNA are not the only chemicals that can do this job. What would probably stay the same? A liquid, a supply of energy, a boundary, and instructions that are copied with small mistakes.
examples: NASA's Dragonfly, a flying robot, is planned to leave for Titan in 2028 and to arrive in 2034.
In 2015, scientists at Cornell worked out on a computer a membrane that might form in liquid methane. A study in 2020 found that it probably would not form.
Carol Cleland and Shelley Copley asked in 2005 whether a second kind of life might exist on Earth unnoticed, because all our tests look for our own kind.
explanations.art: Two imagined cells side by side: one in blue water with a familiar membrane, and one in an orange methane lake under a hazy sky with a differently built membrane.
explanations.context: This card asks which features of Earth's life are truly needed, and which could be different on another world.

explanations.concept: How could we recognise life that is not like ours?
explanations.description: A test that looks for DNA will miss life that uses another chemical. So some scientists look for signs that do not depend on what the life is made of. One idea is called assembly theory, from Lee Cronin, Sara Walker and their teams. They count the smallest number of joining steps needed to build a molecule. Simple molecules form by chance. A molecule that needs more than about 15 steps, and is found in large numbers, was probably made by something that follows instructions. In a study in 2021, only samples from living things held such molecules. Other scientists say the step count has not been tested widely enough. The need for a clear test was shown in 1976. NASA's two Viking landers put food marked with radioactive carbon onto Mars soil. Gas came off the soil, as it would if microbes were eating the food. But another instrument found no carbon molecules in the soil at all. Gilbert Levin and Patricia Straat, who ran the test, argued that it had found life. Most scientists think that harsh chemicals in the soil broke down the food. In 2008 a later lander found such a chemical, perchlorate, in Mars soil.
examples: A protein is a chain that needs hundreds of joining steps, and a cell makes millions of identical copies. That would not happen by chance.
The Viking test gave a positive result that most scientists now explain without life.
A sample from a far world may show something that is neither clearly alive nor clearly not, as a virus does on Earth.

perspectives.who: Lee Cronin, Sara Walker and their teams
perspectives.explanation: Life is the only thing that makes many copies of very complicated molecules. Counting building steps is a test for life that works whatever the life is made of.
Some minerals and some reactions without life can also make complicated things. A single number is too simple, and it has been tried on too few samples.

explanations.art: A Viking lander on red soil with a small scoop, and above it a thought bubble showing a simple molecule and a very complicated one with a question mark.
explanations.context: This card is about how scientists try to test for life without assuming it is built like life on Earth.

explanations.concept: Why the definition matters in practice
explanations.definition: A definition of life is a tool for making decisions, for example about medicines, about space missions and about what laboratories may build.
explanations.description: It can seem that arguing over a word changes nothing. A virus does what a virus does, whatever we call them. But definitions guide what people do. In medicine, knowing that a virus has no chemistry of their own tells doctors what will work. Antibiotics do nothing against viruses. So doctors block a step of the copying. A vaccine teaches the body to make antibodies. An antibody is a protein that sticks to the virus's coat, so that the coat no longer fits the receptor. In space science, the definition decides which instruments fly. A probe built to look for DNA cannot find life made of something else. Space agencies also clean their landers very carefully, so that Earth's microbes are not carried to Mars and mistaken for Mars life. In the laboratory, scientists can now build viruses from chemicals. In 2002, Eckard Wimmer's team built polio virus from mail-ordered pieces of DNA, using the published genome. If a thing can be made from bottled chemicals, was a living thing made? Laws about what may be built depend on such answers.
examples: A doctor does not give an antibiotic for a cold, because a cold is caused by a virus.
India's Covaxin was made from whole coronaviruses that had been inactivated with a chemical.
In 2024, a group of scientists asked the world not to build 'mirror' bacteria, whose molecules would be mirror images of ours, because our bodies' defences might not recognise them.
explanations.art: Three small scenes: a doctor with a vaccine vial, a technician in a clean suit wiping a space lander, and a scientist reading a genome on a screen.
explanations.context: This card explains why the definition of life changes real decisions in medicine, in space science and in laboratories.

agreed.text: A virus is a genome of DNA or RNA inside a protein coat, and some viruses have an envelope of fat as well.
agreed.evidence: Electron microscopes show the particles. X-ray studies, such as Rosalind Franklin's work on tobacco mosaic virus in the 1950s, showed where the RNA sits inside the coat.

agreed.text: A virus can be copied only inside a living cell.
agreed.evidence: In over a hundred years, nobody has grown a virus in food alone. Viruses multiply only when living cells are present, for example in hens' eggs or in dishes of cells.

agreed.text: The genome carries the instructions, and the coat does not.
agreed.evidence: In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase showed that a phage's DNA goes into the bacterium while most of the coat stays outside, and new phages are still made.

agreed.text: Viruses evolve by copying mistakes and selection.
agreed.evidence: Scientists read the genomes of flu viruses and coronaviruses from patients every week. They see new mutations appear, and they see some of them become common.

agreed.text: Every kind of cellular life has viruses: bacteria, plants, fungi and animals, including us.
agreed.evidence: Wherever scientists have looked, from hot springs to the deep sea, they have found viruses that infect the cells living there.

agreed.text: There is no agreed definition of life.
agreed.evidence: In 2011, Edward Trifonov collected 123 different definitions of life from scientific writing. No single one is accepted by everyone.

challenging.claim: A virus is alive, and the infected cell is the virus's living body.
challenging.for: An infected cell feeds, makes energy and builds under the virus's instructions. Calling the particle 'the virus' is like calling a seed 'the plant'.
challenging.against: The ribosomes, the energy and the membrane all belong to the cell. On this view, one cell would be two living beings at once, and it is unclear where one ends.
challenging.context: This card is about the 'virocell' idea: that a virus is alive while inside a cell.

challenging.claim: Viruses are not alive and do not belong on the tree of life.
challenging.for: Viruses have no chemistry of their own, cells do all the copying, and many virus genes were taken from hosts. A tree of life should show cells only.
challenging.against: Viruses have genes found in no cell, they evolve, and they have shaped the genomes of every living being. Leaving them out hides a large part of life's history.
challenging.context: This card is about the view that viruses are products of cells, and not living beings.

challenging.claim: Giant viruses are a fourth great branch of life, beside bacteria, archaea and cells with a nucleus.
challenging.for: Giant viruses have some very old genes for protein-building that seem to branch off on their own.
challenging.against: Later studies found that giant viruses picked up most of these genes from their hosts at different times. Most scientists do not accept a fourth branch.
challenging.context: This card is about the claim that giant viruses form their own branch of the tree of life.

challenging.claim: The Viking landers found life on Mars in 1976.
challenging.who: Gilbert Levin and Patricia Straat, who ran the Viking test
challenging.for: Mars soil gave off gas when fed, and soil that had been heated first did not. That is how soil with microbes behaves on Earth.
challenging.against: No carbon molecules were found in the same soil. Mars soil contains perchlorate, a harsh chemical that can break down the food without any life.
challenging.context: This card is about a test for life on Mars whose result is still argued over.

challenging.claim: Antibiotics help you get over a cold.
challenging.for: People sometimes feel better after taking one. But a cold ends by itself in about a week.
challenging.against: Antibiotics jam parts that only bacteria have. A cold virus has no such parts. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed also helps tough bacteria to spread.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that antibiotics work against viruses. They do not.

challenging.claim: We should stop trying to define life.
challenging.who: Carol Cleland, a philosopher of science, and others
challenging.for: People could not define water correctly until they knew what it is made of. We know only one kind of life, so any definition now is a guess from one example.
challenging.against: Missions and laws need some rule to work with today. A working definition can be useful even if it is later replaced.
challenging.context: This card is about the view that it is too early to define life at all.

big_questions.q: A virus is copied only inside a cell. Is 'alive' something a thing is, or something that happens between a thing and its surroundings?
big_questions.hint: Think of a seed with and without water, and of yourself with and without air. Then think of the virus particle and the infected cell.

big_questions.q: You cannot make your own food, and a virus cannot make their own proteins. Is that a difference of kind, or only of amount?
big_questions.hint: List what you borrow from other living beings in one day. List what a virus borrows. Where would you put Carsonella?

big_questions.q: In the Copying Chain, a pencil line evolved though it did nothing. Does evolution need a living thing, or only copying?
big_questions.hint: Think about who did the copying and who did the choosing. Then ask the same about a virus.

big_questions.q: If scientists build a virus from bottled chemicals, have they made something alive?
big_questions.hint: This was done with polio virus in 2002. Does your answer depend on which definition of life you use?

big_questions.q: We know only one kind of life. How could we tell which of its features are needed and which are accidents?
big_questions.hint: Think of trying to say what a 'fruit' is if you had only ever seen a banana.

big_questions.q: Part of your genome came from viruses, and one of those genes helped build your placenta. Where does 'you' end and 'virus' begin?
big_questions.hint: About 8 of every 100 letters in your genome came from viruses that infected your ancestors.

big_questions.q: If a word like 'alive' has no sharp edge, is it still a useful word?
big_questions.hint: Think of other words with no sharp edge, such as 'tall', 'child' or 'evening'. We still use them every day.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out which part of a virus carries the instructions? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1935, the American chemist Wendell Stanley made crystals of tobacco mosaic virus. He reported that the virus was a pure protein. At that time most scientists believed that genes were made of protein. DNA and RNA seemed too simple, with only four kinds of unit. In 1936, Frederick Bawden and Norman Pirie in England found that the virus also held a little RNA. Few people thought this mattered. In 1952, at Cold Spring Harbor in New York, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase tested the question with phages. Chase was 24 years old. They grew one batch of phages with radioactive sulphur, which goes only into protein. They grew another batch with radioactive phosphorus, which goes only into DNA. They let each batch infect bacteria, and then spun the mixture in a kitchen blender to shake the empty coats off. The sulphur stayed outside the bacteria. The phosphorus went inside, and new phages were made. So the instructions were in the DNA. Hershey shared a Nobel Prize in 1969. Chase did not.
how_we_found_out.who: Wendell Stanley, who crystallised a virus. Frederick Bawden and Norman Pirie, who found its RNA. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase, who showed that the genome carries the instructions.
how_we_found_out.when: 1935 (Stanley's crystals), 1936 (Bawden and Pirie) and 1952 (Hershey and Chase)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a virus is pure protein, and that genes are made of protein. Hershey and Chase showed that a phage's DNA enters the bacterium and directs the making of new phages, while most of the protein coat stays outside.
how_we_found_out.art: A 1950s kitchen blender on a laboratory bench with a flask of cloudy liquid beside it, and a young woman in a lab coat writing in a notebook.

story.title: The Tenth Pot
story.note: A made-up story. Nila, Kathir, Paatti and Dr Vasuki are imagined. The science is real. Tomato mosaic virus is a close relative of tobacco mosaic virus. They spread from plant to plant in sap, on hands and tools, and the leaves show a patchwork of light and dark green about ten days to two weeks later. Washing hands with soap between plants is the advice given to growers. The tomatoes are safe to eat. The reasoning that a poison should get weaker as it is passed on, while this sickness does not, is how Martinus Beijerinck argued in 1898 that the cause multiplies inside the plant. The Agricultural College and Research Institute in Madurai is a real college.
text: Paatti grew ten tomato plants on the terrace in Madurai, in ten grow bags, in one straight row along the parapet wall. Each bag stood on its own two bricks, so that no water ran from one to the next.

Nila had one job in the row. Every morning before school she pinched out the side shoots, the small green shoots that sprout where a leaf joins the stem. Paatti had shown her how. Thumb and finger, a quick snap. Pot one, pot two, pot three, all the way down to pot ten. By the end her fingertips were green and smelled of tomato leaf.
In the first week of the holidays her cousin Kathir came to stay. He was eight, and he followed her up the stairs each morning and gave his opinion on everything.
It was Kathir who saw the first pot. 'This one is ill,' he said.
The new leaves of pot one had come out patchy. Light green and dark green lay side by side on the same leaf, like a kolam drawn in two greens. Some leaves were narrow and curled.
'Something bad is in the soil,' said Kathir. 'A poison. Or bad water.'
That seemed sensible. Paatti scraped off the top soil of pot one and put in fresh compost. She gave pot one water from a separate mug. Nila went on pinching, pot one to pot ten.
Twelve days later pot two had the two greens. A few days after that, pot three. Then pot four.
'The poison is spreading,' said Kathir.
'How?' said Nila. 'The bags do not touch. The water does not run between them. You saw the bricks.'
'Through the air, then.'
'Then why pot two before pot nine? Air does not go down a row in order.'
Kathir had no answer, and for once he said so.

That evening Paatti made rasam, and Nila watched her drop a marble of tamarind into the water. She thought about it all through dinner. Afterwards she lined up ten steel tumblers on the kitchen counter and filled them with water. She squeezed tamarind into the first, until it was brown and sour. Then she poured a spoonful from the first tumbler into the second, a spoonful from the second into the third, and on down the line.
'Taste,' she told Kathir.
He tasted the first and pulled a face. The second was a little sour. The third tasted of almost nothing. By the fifth it was plain water.

'That is what a poison would do,' said Nila. 'Each time it is passed on, there is less of it. Pot one would be very ill. Pot two a little ill. Pot four would be fine.' She took him up to the terrace with a torch. 'Now look.'
Pot four was as patchy as pot one. If anything, the leaves were worse.
'So it is not being shared out,' said Nila slowly. 'It is not getting less. Each plant has as much as the one before. Whatever it is, more of it is being made inside every plant.'
Kathir thought about this. 'Then it is alive,' he said. 'Only living things make more of themselves. It is an insect. Or a mould.'
They borrowed Paatti's reading lens and looked at every leaf of pot four, top and underside. No insects. No eggs. No fluff of mould. Only leaf, in two greens.
'Something too small for the lens,' said Nila. 'Something that goes from pot one to pot two to pot three, in that order, and does not fly.'
She was holding a leaf as she said it. She looked at the leaf. Then she looked at her own thumb and finger, still faintly green from the morning.
'Oh,' she said.
'What?'
'Me. I go from pot one to pot two to pot three. Every morning. In that order. With sap on my fingers.'
Kathir stared at her hand as if it might bite him.

The next morning Nila did the row differently. She carried up a mug of water, a cake of soap and a towel. She began at pot ten, where the leaves were still one clean green. She pinched the shoots of pot ten and washed her hands with soap. Pot nine, and soap again. Pot eight. Kathir timed her and complained that it took four times as long.

They waited. Paatti said waiting was the longest part of gardening. Twelve days passed, and then two weeks. Pots five, six and seven turned patchy, one after another, because Nila had touched them before she understood. Pots eight, nine and ten stayed one clean green.
Paatti rang her old friend Dr Vasuki, who taught at the agricultural college, and held the phone so that both children could hear.

'Tomato mosaic,' said Dr Vasuki at once. 'A virus. Far too small for your lens, or for my microscope either. You worked it out the way the first virus scientists did. A poison thins out. This does not. And you were lucky with the last three pots. By the end of the row there was little sap left on your fingers.'
'So Kathir was right,' said Nila. 'It is alive.'

There was a pause on the line. 'In the dried sap on your fingers,' said Dr Vasuki, 'they do nothing at all. No feeding, no growing. You could keep that sap in a tin for years. Inside a leaf cell, the cell reads their instructions and builds thousands more. Are they alive? People in my college have argued about that since before I was a student. I change my mind about once a year.'
'What about the tomatoes?' asked Kathir. 'Can we eat them?'
'Certainly. These viruses fit a tomato cell. They do not fit yours.'

After the call Nila sat on the terrace step and looked at her washed hands. The same thing had been on her fingers and in the leaf. On her fingers it was like dust. In the leaf it was like a living being. She could not make the two fit into one word, and she found that she did not mind.
Paatti picked six tomatoes from pot one and went down to make rasam.
story.epiphany: A poison gets weaker each time it is passed on, because the same amount is shared out among more plants. The sickness in Paatti's row did not get weaker. So more of it was being made inside every plant. That is the mark of a virus: a cell copies them, so there is always as much as before. Nila also found that the same virus did nothing in dried sap on her fingers and was copied thousands of times inside a leaf cell. Whether to call them alive depends on which of those two places you look at.
ask: A poison gets weaker as it is passed along. Why did the sickness in the row not get weaker?
Why did the sickness move down the row in order, and not jump to pot nine?
Why did washing with soap between plants protect pots eight, nine and ten?
On Nila's fingers the virus did nothing. In the leaf, they were copied. Would you call them alive? Why?
Dr Vasuki changes her mind about once a year. Is that a good or a bad thing in a scientist?

roots.context: We have learned what a virus is, why scientists cannot agree whether viruses are alive, and how NASA defines life. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Copying Chain, the pencil line did no work at all. You did all the copying. Yet the line changed over ten generations, and when you kept the longest copy each time, the line grew steadily longer. A cell copies a virus in the same way. So a thing can evolve without doing any of the work of living.
deep_truth.habit: We think that a thing must first be alive, and that evolving is something living things then do. But evolution needs only copies, small mistakes in the copying, and some copies being copied more than others. That is why NASA's definition needs two separate parts, 'self-sustaining' and 'capable of evolution'. A virus has the second without the first.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Copying Chain, a line copied from copy to copy wandered far from 100 millimetres, and a line chosen for length grew by a few millimetres each generation. The line never copied itself. Flu viruses change every year in the same way, though a virus particle makes no energy and builds nothing.

three.who_am_i: About 8 of every 100 letters in your genome came from viruses that infected your ancestors. One old virus gene helped build the placenta that fed you before you were born.
three.what_is_life: No living being keeps going entirely alone. A virus needs a cell, you need plants, and plants need the Sun. What differs is how much each one borrows.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has stones, prions, viroids, viruses, tiny bacteria and banyan trees, with something in between each pair. The sorting into two boxes, living and non-living, is done by people.

roots.thread: A virus, a bacterium and a grain of sand are built from the same kinds of atoms, and those atoms were made in stars. From that one stock of atoms come things that do no chemistry of their own, things that are copied, and things that copy themselves. There is no step on the way where something new is added from outside. The many kinds of things, and the many kinds of minds, come out of the same one source, and our words 'living' and 'non-living' are a rough sorting of them.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4 (the Buddha's story of the blind men and the elephant, also told by Jain teachers to explain anekantavada, many-sidedness)
teachings.teaching: Several blind men each touch one part of an elephant. One says an elephant is like a pillar, and another says like a fan. Each is right about his part, and wrong to think it is the whole.
teachings.link: One scientist touches the virus particle and says 'a chemical'. Another touches the infected cell and says 'alive'. Each definition of life describes one side of the same thing correctly.

teachings.teaching: The name that can be spoken is not the lasting name. Names are how we divide the world into ten thousand things.
teachings.link: The word 'alive' was in use long before anyone had seen a cell or a virus. The world did not promise to fit the word. A virus shows us where the word runs out.
verse: 道可道，非常道，名可名，非常名。

teachings.source: J.C. Bose, Response in the Living and Non-Living (1902)
teachings.teaching: Jagadish Chandra Bose measured how metals, plants and muscles respond to being struck, tired and poisoned. He found the same kinds of response in all three, and wrote that he could find no sharp break between the living and the non-living.
teachings.link: Bose's measurements of plants were real and ahead of their time. His wider idea is not accepted by most scientists. Viruses, viroids and prions, which he never knew, sit exactly where he said there was no break.

science.text: About 8 percent of the human genome came from viruses, and the placenta is built with a gene that was once a virus's envelope gene (Mi and others, Nature, 2000).
Viruses evolve by the same copying mistakes and selection as every living being.
Whether a virus is alive, and whether the infected cell should count as the living virus.
Whether anything like awareness goes with the sensing and signalling that viruses and single cells do. Nobody knows how to test this yet.

other_view.who: Most biologists, and thinkers of the Charvaka school in ancient India
other_view.view: Many biologists say the line is real and sharp enough. A thing with ribosomes and its own supply of energy is alive, and everything else is not. A few odd cases at the border do not remove the border, just as dusk does not make day and night the same. Most brain scientists also think that awareness needs a brain. The Charvaka thinkers taught that only matter exists, and that life and mind appear when matter is arranged in the right way, as the power to make people drunk appears when grain is fermented.

practice.title: What am I borrowing right now?
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. The oxygen in this breath was let out by a plant or by a tiny being in the sea. Breathe out. Now feel your stomach. Your last meal was grown by plants and cooked by someone. Tiny beings in your gut are helping you to digest it right now. Now hold your breath gently and count to ten. Feel how soon you need the outside again. Breathe normally. Open your eyes. Tell me one thing you did today with no help from any other living being.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. A plant or a sea microbe made that oxygen. Feel your stomach. Plants grew your last meal. Hold your breath and count to ten. Feel how soon you need air. Breathe again. What did you do today with no help from any living being?

ask: A virus is copied only inside a cell, and you stay alive only with air, food and water from outside. So is being alive something you have, or something you are given all the time?
A pencil line can evolve if someone copies it. Does that make evolution less special, or copying more special?
People made the word 'alive' before they knew about cells or viruses. If the world does not fit the word, which one should change?

games.title: Three Tokens: test 20 cases against NASA's definition
games.context: This is a card game about NASA's definition of life. Each card names one thing. You lay down a token for each part of the definition that the thing passes, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 20 case cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A cold virus particle on a door handle
items.b: C and E. They are chemical and their kind evolves. They do not keep themselves going, so no S.

items.f: A nose cell that a cold virus has entered
items.b: C, S and E. The infected cell feeds, makes energy and builds viruses. Some scientists say this is the living stage of the virus. Argue it.

items.f: A bacterium in a bowl of curd
items.b: C, S and E. They take in milk sugar, build their own parts, divide and evolve.

items.f: A candle flame
items.b: C and S. A flame is chemical and keeps going while wax lasts. A flame has no instructions to pass on, so no E.

items.f: A salt crystal growing in a salt pan
items.b: C only. A crystal adds more salt to its outside. It uses no energy to build itself and has no instructions that vary.

items.f: A mule, who cannot have young
items.b: C and S for certain. One mule cannot evolve, but horses and donkeys do. The definition is about a kind over generations. Argue E.

items.f: A dry ragi seed kept in a dabba for a year
items.b: C and E. The seed is paused, so S is 'not now, but they can'. Every biologist calls the seed alive. Argue S.

items.f: A computer virus
items.b: None. It is a pattern in a machine, with no chemistry of its own. It makes exact copies and changes only when a person rewrites it.

items.f: A chain message that says 'send this to 10 people'
items.b: E only, and argue it. People copy it, change it a little, and the catchier versions spread more. It is not chemical and does not sustain itself.

items.f: A prion: a wrongly folded protein that makes others fold wrongly
items.b: C only for most scientists. A prion has no genome. A 2010 study found that prion types can change and be selected, so E can be argued.

items.f: A viroid: a bare loop of RNA that plant cells copy
items.b: C and E. A viroid has no coat and makes no protein, yet their kind evolves. No S.

items.f: A mimivirus particle with about 1,000 genes
items.b: C and E. Even with 1,000 genes, a mimivirus has no ribosomes and makes no energy. No S.

items.f: A Carsonella bacterium, who lives only inside insect cells
items.b: C and E, and S in part. They have ribosomes but take most of what they need from the host. Biologists call them alive. Argue S.

items.f: A human red blood cell
items.b: C and S. A red blood cell uses sugar and keeps going for about 120 days. They have no genome and never divide, so no E.

items.f: A mitochondrion inside one of your cells
items.b: C and E. A mitochondrion has their own small genome and divides, but cannot live outside a cell. Lynn Margulis argued in 1967 that their ancestors were free bacteria, and DNA later showed she was right.

items.f: A worker honeybee, who almost never has young
items.b: C and S for certain. She almost never has young of her own, but her hive's kind evolves through her mother, the queen. Argue E.

items.f: A robot that builds exact copies of itself from scrap (imagined)
items.b: Argue all three. Is a machine a 'chemical system'? It may sustain itself. With exact copies, it cannot evolve.

items.f: A water bear dried up in a tuft of moss
items.b: C and E. Dried, a water bear does almost no chemistry, so S is 'not now, but they can'. Argue S.

items.f: The whole Earth: air, sea, rocks and living things together
items.b: C and S. Earth runs on sunlight, and its living things and rocks together keep the air fairly steady. There is only one Earth and it makes no copies, so no E.

items.f: The Sun
items.b: S only. The Sun keeps itself going for thousands of millions of years, by nuclear reactions and not chemical ones. The Sun makes no copies with small changes.

printables.title: 3 tokens for each player (make a set for everyone)

rules: Each player takes three tokens: C, S and E. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, case side up.
One player reads the top card aloud.
Each player secretly chooses the tokens that the case passes, and hides them under a hand. On the count of three, everyone shows.
Turn the card over and read the back. A player whose tokens match the back scores one point.
If the back says 'argue', any player who gives a sensible reason for their choice scores the point.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: score one point for each card you match. Try to reach 13 out of 20, then play again another day.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. 2. Read NASA's definition aloud: life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. 3. Go through the three tokens with a curd bacterium as the example.
flow.say: NASA's definition has three parts. C is for chemical system. S is for self-sustaining. E is for able to evolve. A curd bacterium passes all three.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. C means chemical. S means keeps itself going. E means its kind can evolve.

ask.q: Why does a curd bacterium pass all three?
good: They are made of chemicals that act on each other.
They take in milk sugar and build their own parts.
They divide, and the copies can differ a little.

flow.context: This is the first step of Three Tokens. Here you make the tokens and learn what each one stands for.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Everyone secretly chooses tokens. 3. Count to three and show. 4. Turn the card and read the back. 5. Give the points, and talk about any 'argue' card.
flow.say: For each card, ask three questions. Is it made of chemicals acting on each other? Does it keep itself going? Can its kind change over generations?
flow.kid: Read the card. Choose your tokens in secret. Show them on three.
flow.parent: The backs give the usual answer, and several cards have no settled answer. Reward a good reason. The cards that pass exactly two parts are the most interesting ones.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Three Tokens. Here you play through the 20 cards.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Sort the cards into four heaps by how many parts they pass: none, one, two or three. 3. Ask which heap the virus is in, and what else is there.
flow.say: Look at the heap that passes two parts. Which part does each one fail?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards by how many parts they pass. Which heap is the virus in? What else is there?

check.q: A candle flame and a cold virus each pass two of NASA's three parts. Which part does each one fail?
options: Both fail 'chemical system'
The flame fails 'evolve', the virus fails 'self-sustaining'
The flame fails 'self-sustaining', the virus fails 'evolve'
check.why: A flame keeps itself going but has no instructions to pass on, so a flame cannot evolve. A virus's kind evolves, but a virus particle does not keep themselves going. So the definition needs both parts: each one alone lets in something that few people call alive.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Tokens. Here you sort the cards by how many parts they pass.

games.title: Who Fits Whom? Match each virus to their host
games.context: This is a matching game about viruses and their hosts. A virus can enter only a cell whose receptor fits their coat. So every virus has their own hosts, and most viruses cannot infect humans at all.

items: VIRUS: Tobacco mosaic virus. A stiff rod. Spreads in sap on hands and tools.
HOST: Tomato, tobacco and chilli plants
VIRUS: T4 phage. Looks like a tiny moon lander. Injects DNA through a tail.
HOST: The gut bacterium E. coli
VIRUS: Rabies virus. Bullet-shaped. Travels in saliva through a bite.
HOST: Dogs, bats, humans and other mammals
VIRUS: Measles virus. Spreads through the air. A vaccine protects against them.
VIRUS: Bhendi yellow vein mosaic virus. Turns leaf veins yellow.
HOST: Ladies' finger plants, carried there by whiteflies
VIRUS: Banana bunchy top virus. Makes the top leaves short, narrow and bunched.
HOST: Banana plants, carried there by aphids
VIRUS: White spot syndrome virus. Leaves white spots on the shell.
VIRUS: Foot-and-mouth disease virus. Causes blisters on mouths and hooves.
HOST: Cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep and pigs
VIRUS: Mimivirus. A giant virus with about 1,000 genes.
HOST: An amoeba, a single-celled being that lives in water
VIRUS: Sputnik. A small virus who needs a giant virus.
HOST: The copying factory of a mimivirus, inside an amoeba
VIRUS: Pod borer virus (HaNPV). Farmers spray them on chickpea and cotton.
HOST: Caterpillars of the pod borer moth
VIRUS: Canine parvovirus. Vets vaccinate puppies against them.
HOST: Dogs, and puppies most of all

printables.title: Answer sheet: the 12 pairs
items: Tobacco mosaic virus: tomato, tobacco and chilli plants
T4 phage: the gut bacterium E. coli
Rabies virus: dogs, bats, humans and other mammals
Bhendi yellow vein mosaic virus: ladies' finger plants, by whiteflies
Banana bunchy top virus: banana plants, by aphids
White spot syndrome virus: prawns, shrimps and crabs
Foot-and-mouth disease virus: cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep and pigs
Sputnik: the copying factory of a mimivirus
Pod borer virus: caterpillars of the pod borer moth

rules: Round 1, face up. Lay all 24 cards face up. Take turns to pick a virus card and the host card you think fits. Check the answer sheet. A right pair scores one point and is taken off the table. A wrong pair goes back.
Round 2, face down. Shuffle all 24 cards and lay them face down in a grid of 4 rows and 6 columns.
On your turn, turn over two cards. If they are a virus and their own host, keep the pair and take another turn. If not, turn them back.
When all the cards are taken, the player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to clear the grid. Try to beat your count next time.

setup.art: Twenty-four small cards laid face up on a table, half headed VIRUS and half headed HOST, with a child holding one of each.
setup.caption: 1. Round 1: lay the cards face up and pair each virus with their host.

setup.art: The same cards face down in a grid of four rows and six columns, with two cards turned over.
setup.caption: 2. Round 2: lay the cards face down. Turn over two at a time and look for a pair.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. 2. Lay the 12 virus cards face up. 3. Ask how many of these twelve can infect a human, and why your child thinks so.
flow.say: Here are twelve real viruses. How many of them do you think can infect a human? Why?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay out the 12 virus cards. Guess how many can infect a human. Say why.
flow.parent: The answer is two: rabies and measles. Most children guess far more.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Fits Whom?. Here you cut out the cards and guess how many of the viruses can infect humans.

flow.do: 1. Lay all 24 cards face up. 2. Take turns to pair a virus with a host, using the clue on the card. 3. Check each pair on the answer sheet. 4. Go on until all 12 pairs are found.
flow.say: Read the clue on the virus card. Which host fits? If you are not sure, which hosts can you rule out?
flow.kid: Lay all the cards face up. Pick a virus and the host you think fits. Check the answer sheet. Keep the right pairs.

ask.q: Why can the banana virus not infect the person who eats the banana?
good: The virus's coat fits a receptor in banana cells, and our cells have no such receptor.
The key does not fit any lock on our cells.

flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Who Fits Whom?. Here you play round 1, with the cards face up.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle and lay the cards face down in 4 rows of 6. 2. Take turns to turn over two cards. 3. Keep a pair if the virus matches the host. 4. Count the pairs at the end.
flow.say: Now it is a memory game. A pair is a virus and their own host. What decides which host a virus can enter?
flow.kid: Lay the cards face down in 4 rows of 6. Turn over two. Keep them if the virus fits the host. Count your pairs at the end.

check.q: The measles virus infects humans but not dogs. Why?
options: Dogs are too clean
The virus's coat fits a receptor on human cells only
Measles viruses dislike dogs' food
check.why: A virus can enter only a cell whose receptor fits their coat, as a key fits a lock. The measles virus fits receptors on human cells. A dog's cells have no receptor of that exact shape, so the virus cannot get in.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Fits Whom?. Here you play round 2, with the cards face down, and talk about why each virus has their own hosts.

experiments.title: The Copying Chain: what happens when copies are copied?
experiments.context: In this experiment you copy a pencil line by eye, again and again. In one chain, each new line is a copy of the last copy. In part 2 you make three copies each time and keep the longest. You will find out whether copying mistakes pile up, and how keeping the longest copy can make a line grow.
experiments.question: If a line is copied from copy to copy for ten generations, how far does it change? And what happens if, in every generation, only the longest of three copies is copied again?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After ten copies of copies, will the last line be the same length as the first, a little different or very different? Will the copies made straight from the original end up closer to it, or further away? In part 2, where you keep the longest of three each time, how long will the line be after eight generations? Write your three guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: The same person draws every line, with the same pencil, on slips of the same size. Look at the parent line for a slow count of three, turn it face down, and only then draw. Never lay two slips side by side while drawing. In part 1, change only what is copied: the last copy in chain A, and the original in set B. Do not measure any line until all the drawing is finished, so that the numbers cannot guide your hand.
results_table: Chain A: copy of the last copy (mm)
Set B: copy of the original (mm)

materials.item: sheets of A4 paper, used on one side is fine
a ruler marked in millimetres, 30 centimetres long
a pencil and an eraser
scissors
a notebook for the table and the graph

experiments.safety: Cut the paper strips with care, or ask a grown-up to cut them.

schedule.what: Cut the slips. Draw chain A and set B. Draw part 2, keeping the longest of three each time. Measure every line, fill in the table and draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with every measurement. Draw a line graph with the generation along the bottom and the length up the side, with one line for chain A and one for part 2. Mark set B as dots. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: part 2, keeping the longest of three copies
example_chart.y: Length of the line that was kept (mm)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A sheet of A4 paper cut lengthwise into six long strips, with a ruler and a pencil beside them, and one strip showing a straight pencil line labelled 'Original, 100 mm'.
setup.caption: 1. Cut each sheet into 6 long strips. On one strip, rule a line exactly 100 millimetres long. This is the original.

setup.art: A child looking at a strip with a pencil line on it, then the same strip turned face down while the child draws a line freehand on a fresh strip.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the parent line for a count of three. Turn it face down. Draw a line of the same length on a new strip.

setup.art: A row of ten numbered strips, each with a pencil line of slightly different length, with an arrow from each strip to the next.
setup.caption: 3. Chain A: each new line is a copy of the last copy.

setup.art: Three strips laid side by side with their left ends lined up, and a hand picking the strip with the longest line.
setup.caption: 4. Part 2: draw three copies, line up their ends, and keep the longest as the next parent.

flow.do: 1. Cut 8 sheets of A4 paper lengthwise into 6 strips each. 2. On one strip, rule a straight line exactly 100 millimetres long. 3. Write 'Original' on the back. 4. Number the backs of ten strips A1 to A10, and ten more B1 to B10.
flow.say: We are going to copy this line by eye, many times. First we need a pile of strips and one line that is exactly 100 millimetres long.
flow.kid: Cut the paper into long strips. Rule one line 100 mm long. Write 'Original' on its back. Number ten strips A1 to A10. Number ten more B1 to B10.
flow.parent: Each strip is about 3.5 centimetres wide and 30 centimetres long. You need about 45 strips in all. Paper already used on one side is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Copying Chain. Here you cut the paper strips and rule the original line.

flow.do: 1. Explain chain A and set B. 2. Ask for the first two guesses and their reasons. 3. Explain part 2. 4. Ask for the third guess and its reason. 5. Write all three down.
flow.say: In chain A you copy the last copy each time. In set B you copy the original each time. Which will end closer to 100 millimetres? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how much the line changes in chain A. Guess which stays closer, A or B. Guess how long the line gets in part 2. Say why each time. Write it down.

good: Small mistakes will add up in chain A, because each copy starts from the last mistake.
In set B every copy starts from the right length, so the mistakes cannot add up.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the mistakes to cancel out, so that chain A ends near 100.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 7 of the Copying Chain. This step is for guessing. You guess before any line is copied.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks at the original for a slow count of three. 2. They turn it face down. 3. They draw a freehand line of the same length on strip A1. 4. They copy A1 onto A2 in the same way, then A2 onto A3, up to A10.
flow.say: Look at the line and count slowly to three. Turn it over. Now draw a line of the same length. Each new line is copied from the one you have just drawn.
flow.kid: Look at the line for a count of three. Turn it face down. Draw the same length on the next strip. Copy each new line from the last one.
flow.parent: Draw freehand, without the ruler. Keep the finished strips face down in a pile, so only the newest parent is ever seen.
flow.context: This is step 3 of 7 of the Copying Chain. Here you draw chain A, where each line is a copy of the last copy.

flow.do: 1. Put the original face up. 2. Your child looks for a count of three and turns it face down. 3. They draw the line on strip B1. 4. They repeat this for B2 to B10, looking at the original each time.
flow.say: Now every line is copied from the original. Look, count to three, turn it over and draw. Do this ten times.
flow.kid: Now copy the original every time. Look, count to three, turn it over, draw. Do this for B1 to B10.
flow.parent: Set B is the control. It shows how big one copying mistake is, when mistakes cannot add up.
flow.context: This is step 4 of 7 of the Copying Chain. Here you draw set B, where every line is a copy of the original.

flow.do: 1. Start from the original again. 2. Your child draws three copies of it on three strips, looking afresh before each one. 3. Line up the left ends of the three lines and keep the longest. 4. Write 'P1' on its back. 5. Draw three copies of P1 and keep the longest as P2. 6. Go on until P8.
flow.say: This time the rule is that only the longest copy gets copied again. Draw three copies, keep the longest, and copy that one. We do this for eight generations.
flow.kid: Draw three copies of the parent. Line up their ends. Keep the longest and name it P1. Copy P1 three times. Keep the longest again. Go on to P8.

ask.q: You are trying to draw every line the same length. So can the line still get longer?
good: Yes, because some copies come out a bit long by mistake, and we keep those.
Each kept mistake becomes the new starting point.

flow.parent: Your child should still try to copy each line exactly. They must not draw longer on purpose. Put the two copies that were not kept in a separate pile.
flow.context: This is step 5 of 7 of the Copying Chain. This is part 2. Here you draw three copies each time and keep only the longest.

flow.do: 1. Now bring out the ruler. 2. Measure A1 to A10, B1 to B10 and P1 to P8 in millimetres, from end to end in a straight line. 3. Write each length in the table. 4. For chain A and for set B, find the line that is furthest from 100 millimetres.
flow.say: Now we measure. Which line in chain A is furthest from 100 millimetres? Which line in set B is furthest? Which of the two gaps is bigger?
flow.kid: Measure every line in millimetres. Write each one in the table. Find the line furthest from 100 in chain A. Find the furthest in set B.
flow.parent: Set B lines usually stay within about 10 millimetres of 100. Chain A usually wanders 15 to 40 millimetres away. A chain can also wander away and come back. If chain A ends within 5 millimetres of 100, look at its furthest point, or draw a second chain.
flow.context: This is step 6 of 7 of the Copying Chain. Here you measure every line and fill in the table.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a line graph of chain A and of part 2. 2. Ask for the three sentences. 3. Ask who did the copying and who did the choosing. 4. Only then read the explanation cards together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why. Then tell me this. Did the line copy itself? Who copied it, and who chose the longest?
flow.kid: Draw the graph, or lay the strips side by side in order. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Why did chain A wander further than set B?
good: In chain A each mistake was copied into the next line, so mistakes added up.
In set B each copy started again from the true length.

ask.q: In part 2 the line got longer every generation. Did the line do anything to make that happen?
good: No. I copied it and I chose the longest.
It only needed copies, small mistakes and a rule about which copy is kept.
