flow.parent: In part 2, expect a gain of about 3 to 8 millimetres in most generations, so about 130 to 160 millimetres at P8. This is the main idea of the unit. A virus genome is copied by a cell, with small mistakes, and the virus's surroundings 'keep' the copies that get into more cells.

check.q: In part 2 of the Copying Chain, the line grew longer each generation. What made it grow?
options: The pencil line stretched by itself
Small copying mistakes, and keeping the longest copy
The child drew longer on purpose
check.why: Each copy came out a little long or a little short by mistake. Keeping the longest copy each time kept the 'long' mistakes and threw the others away. The line did nothing itself. Choosing 'drew longer on purpose' misses that the child tried to copy exactly, and the change came from the choosing.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Copying Chain. Here you draw the graph, explain your results and think about who did the copying.

experiments.title: Two Liquids: what can water dissolve, and what can oil dissolve?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stir salt, sugar, turmeric and ghee into water, and then into cooking oil. You find out which liquid dissolves which. This matters for life on other worlds, because the lakes on Saturn's moon Titan are oily liquids, with no liquid water.
experiments.question: Does cooking oil dissolve the same things that water dissolves?
experiments.predict: Guess first, for each of the four things: salt, sugar, turmeric and ghee. Will it dissolve in water? Will it dissolve in oil? Write eight guesses as a tick or a cross, and give a reason for at least two of them.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the liquid. Use the same amount of liquid in every glass, 2 tablespoons. Use the same small amount of each thing, a quarter of a teaspoon. Stir each glass 30 times, and wait the same 5 minutes before you look. Use a clean, dry spoon for each glass, because one drop of water in the oil changes the result.

materials.item: small clear glasses or clear plastic cups (or use 4 and wash and dry them between rounds)
drinking water
cooking oil with little colour, such as sunflower or rice bran oil
table salt, sugar and turmeric powder
materials.qty: a quarter teaspoon of each, twice

materials.item: ghee, butter or vanaspati
dry teaspoons, or one spoon wiped dry each time
a sheet of white paper, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilt oil at once, because an oily floor is slippery. The oil can be strained and used for cooking the same day.

schedule.what: Guess. Stir four things into water and the same four into oil. Wait, look and fill in the table. Work out the pattern.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each glass, write what you saw: gone and clear, clear but coloured, cloudy, lying at the bottom, or floating. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and what pattern you found.

example_chart.title: Made-up example of a finished table
example_chart.note: This table is an example. Write what you really see in your own glasses.

setup.art: Eight small clear glasses in two rows of four on a table, the back row holding water and the front row holding pale yellow oil, with a label in front of each pair: salt, sugar, turmeric, ghee.
setup.caption: 1. Set out 8 glasses. Put 2 tablespoons of water in four, and 2 tablespoons of oil in four.

setup.art: A child's hand tipping a quarter teaspoon of white salt into a small glass of water, with a dry spoon ready to stir.
setup.caption: 2. Add a quarter teaspoon of one thing to a glass of water, and the same to a glass of oil. Stir each 30 times.

setup.art: A child holding a sheet of white paper behind a glass of yellow oil and a glass of cloudy yellow water, comparing them.
setup.caption: 3. Wait 5 minutes. Hold white paper behind each glass. Is the liquid clear or cloudy? Is anything lying at the bottom?

flow.do: 1. Set out 8 clear glasses in two rows of four. 2. Put 2 tablespoons of water in each glass of the back row. 3. Put 2 tablespoons of oil in each glass of the front row. 4. Write salt, sugar, turmeric and ghee on four slips and lay one in front of each pair.
flow.say: We have two liquids, water and oil. We will stir the same four things into each. Let's set out the glasses first.
flow.kid: Set out 8 glasses in two rows. Put 2 tablespoons of water in four. Put 2 tablespoons of oil in four. Label the four pairs.
flow.parent: The glasses and spoons must be dry before the oil goes in. If you have only 4 glasses, do the water round first, then wash and dry them well.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Liquids. Here you set out the eight glasses.

flow.do: 1. Ask what 'dissolve' means. 2. Ask for the eight guesses. 3. Ask for a reason for at least two of them. 4. Your child writes the guesses down.
flow.say: When something dissolves, it spreads through the liquid in pieces too small to see. Which of these four will dissolve in water? Which in oil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each thing. Will it dissolve in water? Will it dissolve in oil? Write a tick or a cross. Give a reason for two of them.

good: Salt and sugar vanish in water when we cook, so I think water dissolves them.
Ghee is oily, so I think it will mix with oil and not with water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Most children are sure about water, and are guessing about oil.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 6 of Two Liquids. This step is for guessing. You guess before anything is stirred in.

flow.do: 1. Add a quarter teaspoon of salt to the first glass of water. 2. Stir 30 times. 3. Do the same with sugar, turmeric and ghee in the other three glasses of water. 4. Leave them to stand.
flow.say: Stir each one 30 times, and count aloud. What do you see happening in each glass as you stir?
flow.kid: Add salt to the first glass of water. Stir 30 times. Do the same with sugar, turmeric and ghee. Leave them to stand.
flow.parent: In a cold room, ghee stays in hard lumps in water. That is fine. It is a real result.
flow.context: This is step 3 of 6 of Two Liquids. Here you stir the four things into the water.

flow.do: 1. Take a dry spoon. 2. Add a quarter teaspoon of salt to the first glass of oil and stir 30 times. 3. Do the same with sugar, turmeric and ghee. 4. Leave them to stand, and note the time.
flow.say: Now the same four things go into oil, with a dry spoon. Watch closely. Is the oil doing what the water did?
flow.kid: Take a dry spoon. Add salt to the first glass of oil. Stir 30 times. Do the same with sugar, turmeric and ghee. Note the time.
flow.parent: If the ghee is hard, it mixes into the oil slowly. Give that glass 10 minutes and stir again.
flow.context: This is step 4 of 6 of Two Liquids. Here you stir the same four things into the oil.

flow.do: 1. Wait 5 minutes from the last stir. 2. Hold white paper behind each glass. 3. For each glass, your child says whether the liquid is clear or cloudy, and whether anything lies at the bottom or floats. 4. They fill in the table.
flow.say: Look through the side of each glass. Is the liquid clear or cloudy? Has it changed colour? Is anything lying at the bottom or floating on top?
flow.kid: Wait 5 minutes. Hold white paper behind each glass. Is the liquid clear or cloudy? Is anything at the bottom? Fill in the table.
flow.parent: Turmeric is the hard one. In both liquids some powder settles, because turmeric powder is mostly plant fibre and starch. Look at the liquid above the powder. The oil is clear and strongly yellow, because the yellow colour has dissolved. The water is cloudy and pale, because fine bits are floating in it without dissolving.
flow.context: This is step 5 of 6 of Two Liquids. Here you wait, look carefully and fill in the table.

flow.do: 1. Ask for the three sentences. 2. Ask what pattern your child sees in the table. 3. Ask what a living cell on a world with oily lakes could not use. 4. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: What did you think would happen, and what did you see? Which things did water dissolve, and which did oil dissolve? Do you see a pattern?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Which things did water dissolve? Which did oil dissolve?

good: Water dissolved salt and sugar, and oil did not.
Oil dissolved the ghee and the yellow of the turmeric, and water did not.

ask.q: Titan's lakes are an oily liquid with no water. Could a living thing there use salt and sugar as our cells do?
good: No, because salt and sugar would lie at the bottom and never meet.
It would need other chemicals that dissolve in that liquid.

flow.parent: Chemists say 'like dissolves like'. Water dissolves salts and sugars. Oily liquids dissolve fats and oily colours. Your cells are full of salts, sugars, proteins and DNA dissolved in water. The membrane round each cell is made of fat, which is why the water inside does not dissolve it away.

check.q: In Two Liquids, salt vanished in water but lay at the bottom of the oil. What does that tell us about life in an oily lake?
options: It could use salt, if it stirred harder
It would need chemicals that dissolve in that liquid
Life is impossible without salt
check.why: Chemicals react when they meet, and they meet easily only when dissolved. Salt does not dissolve in oily liquids, however long you stir. So life in such a lake would need different chemicals. Choosing 'impossible' goes too far: nobody knows whether other chemicals could do the job.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Liquids. Here you look for the pattern and connect it to cells and to other worlds.

activities.title: Live, Killed or Inactivated? The words on a vaccination card
activities.context: In this activity you look at your own vaccination card and sort the vaccines against viruses into three kinds. You notice that doctors use the words 'live' and 'killed' for viruses, and you ask whether those words fit.

materials.item: your vaccination card or booklet (if you cannot find it, use the list in step 1)
a pencil and a notebook

activities.record: Make a table with three columns: 'live, weakened virus', 'inactivated virus' and 'one part of a virus'. Write each of your vaccines against viruses in the right column.

setup.art: A child and a mother looking at an open Indian vaccination booklet on a table, with rows of vaccine names and dates.
setup.caption: 1. Find your vaccination card and read the names of the vaccines.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns headed 'live, weakened virus', 'inactivated virus' and 'one part of a virus', with vaccine names written under each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the vaccines against viruses into three columns.

setup.art: A child circling the words 'live' and 'killed' on a notebook page, with a question mark drawn beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Circle the words that belong to living things. Do they fit a virus?

flow.do: 1. Find the vaccination card. 2. Read the names aloud together. 3. Use this list to sort them. Polio drops, measles and rubella, and rotavirus drops hold live, weakened viruses. The polio injection, the rabies injection and Covaxin hold inactivated viruses. The hepatitis B vaccine holds one protein of the virus. 4. Leave out BCG, DPT and tetanus, which are against bacteria.
flow.say: A vaccine shows your body a virus safely, so your body learns to recognise them. Let's see which kind each of your vaccines is.
flow.kid: Find your vaccination card. Read the names. Sort the virus vaccines into three groups: live weakened virus, inactivated virus, one part of a virus. Use the list to help you.
flow.parent: On the card, polio drops are OPV, the polio injection is IPV or fIPV, and measles and rubella is MR or MMR. 'Weakened' means the virus has been changed so that they are copied only a little and cause no illness in a healthy child.
flow.context: This is the first step of Live, Killed or Inactivated?. Here you read the vaccine names and sort them into three columns.

flow.do: 1. Point to the words 'live' and 'killed' or 'inactivated'. 2. Ask your child what they think 'inactivated' means. 3. Ask whether a virus can be killed, and why. 4. Listen to the whole answer before saying anything.
flow.say: Doctors call some vaccines 'live' and others 'killed' or 'inactivated'. What do you think 'inactivated' means? Can a virus be killed? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the words 'live' and 'inactivated'. What might 'inactivated' mean?

ask.q: Can a virus be killed? Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because a virus makes you ill and can be stopped.
I am not sure, because you can only kill something that is alive, and I do not know if a virus is.

flow.parent: Do not settle it. The whole unit is about this question. 'Inactivated' means the virus has been damaged, by heat or a chemical, so that no cell can copy them.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Live, Killed or Inactivated?. Here you guess why doctors say 'inactivated' and whether a virus can be killed.

flow.do: 1. Read out these words that scientists use about viruses: live, killed, survive, attack, particle, crystal, inactivate, assemble. 2. Your child sorts them into 'words for living beings' and 'words for chemicals'. 3. Ask what it means that both kinds are used.
flow.say: Here are eight words that scientists use about viruses. Which ones do we use for living beings? Which do we use for chemicals? What does it tell you that they use both?
flow.kid: Sort the eight words. Which are for living beings? Which are for chemicals? Scientists use both for viruses. What does that tell you?
flow.think: If you had to choose one word for what soap does to a virus, which would you choose, and why?

check.q: A vaccine label says 'inactivated virus'. What has been done to the virus?
options: They have been made bigger
They have been damaged so no cell can copy them
They have been turned into bacteria
check.why: An inactivated virus has been damaged by heat or a chemical, so that no cell can copy them. Their coat is still there, and the body learns to recognise it. Choosing 'turned into bacteria' mixes up two very different things: a bacterium is a cell, and a virus is not.

flow.context: This is the last step of Live, Killed or Inactivated?. Here you sort the words people use for viruses, and see that both kinds are used.

activities.title: Walk the Scale: how small is a virus?
activities.context: In this activity you build a paper model in which everything is 10,000 times bigger than in real life. A virus becomes a dot, a bacterium becomes a paper strip, and you become taller than a mountain. You will find out how many flu viruses fit across one of your own cells.

materials.item: a sheet of newspaper and a sheet of plain paper
a ruler and a measuring tape
a pen, scissors and sticky tape

activities.record: Write the scale table in your notebook: each thing, its real size and its model size. Then write one sentence about what surprised you.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a pen dot labelled 'flu virus, 1 mm', a paper strip 2 centimetres long labelled 'bacterium', and a paper circle 7.5 centimetres across labelled 'red blood cell'.
setup.caption: 1. Make the virus, the bacterium and the red blood cell at 10,000 times their real size.

setup.art: A newspaper circle 60 centimetres across on the floor labelled 'cheek cell', with the small paper pieces placed on it.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a cheek cell 60 centimetres across from newspaper, and lay the others on it.

setup.art: A child holding one end of a measuring tape stretched 3 metres across a room, with a label 'one grain of salt'.
setup.caption: 3. Measure 3 metres across the room. That is one grain of salt at this scale.

flow.do: 1. Put one grain of salt on a dark plate. 2. Ask how many flu viruses, side by side, would cross it. 3. Write the guess down. 4. Explain the scale: everything in the model is 10,000 times bigger. A flu virus is about 100 nanometres across, and a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. So the flu virus becomes a dot 1 millimetre across.
flow.say: Here is one grain of salt. How many flu viruses in a row would it take to cross it? Make a guess, and say why.
flow.kid: Look at one grain of salt. How many flu viruses would cross it? Guess, and say why. Write your guess down.
flow.parent: The answer is about 3,000. Most guesses are far smaller. In the model, everything is 10,000 times its real size.
flow.context: This is the first step of Walk the Scale. Here you guess how many viruses fit across a grain of salt.

flow.do: 1. Draw a dot 1 millimetre across for a flu virus. 2. Draw a dot 7 millimetres across for a mimivirus. 3. Cut a strip 2 centimetres long for an E. coli bacterium. 4. Cut a circle 7.5 centimetres across for a red blood cell. 5. Cut a circle 60 centimetres across from newspaper for a cheek cell.
flow.say: Let's make each one 10,000 times bigger. The flu virus is a dot. How big do you think the bacterium will be? And one of your cheek cells?
flow.kid: Draw a 1 mm dot for a flu virus. Draw a 7 mm dot for a mimivirus. Cut a 2 cm strip for a bacterium. Cut a 7.5 cm circle and a 60 cm circle for two cells.
flow.parent: Real sizes: flu virus 100 nanometres, mimivirus about 700 nanometres, E. coli 2 micrometres, red blood cell 7.5 micrometres, cheek cell about 60 micrometres. A micrometre is 1,000 nanometres.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Walk the Scale. Here you make the paper models of a virus, a bacterium and two cells.

flow.do: 1. Lay the small pieces on the newspaper cell. 2. Measure 3 metres across the room for the grain of salt. 3. Work out your child's height at this scale. Multiply their height in metres by 10. That gives kilometres. 4. Name a place that far from home.
flow.say: A grain of salt would be 3 metres across. And you? You are about 1.3 metres tall. At this scale you would be 13 kilometres tall. Where is 13 kilometres from here?
flow.kid: Lay the virus on the big cell. Measure 3 metres for the grain of salt. Work out your own height in the model. Name a place that far away.

ask.q: A school microscope shows a bacterium but not a flu virus. Look at your model. Why might that be?
good: The virus is twenty times smaller than the bacterium.
The virus is too small for light to show.

check.q: In Walk the Scale, a flu virus was a 1 millimetre dot and a cheek cell was 60 centimetres across. What does that show?
options: A virus is about as big as a cell
Hundreds of viruses fit across one cell
A cell is smaller than a virus
check.why: 60 centimetres is 600 millimetres, so 600 flu viruses in a row would cross one cheek cell. A virus is far smaller than the cells that copy them. Choosing 'as big as a cell' usually comes from pictures that draw viruses and cells the same size.

flow.context: This is the last step of Walk the Scale. Here you measure out a grain of salt and yourself at the same scale.

activities.title: Pori Rafts: can parts put themselves together?
activities.context: In this activity you scatter puffed rice on a bowl of water and watch the grains pull together into rafts with no help. It is a model of how the parts of a virus's coat, called coat proteins, join up by themselves inside a cell.

materials.item: a wide bowl or a steel plate with a rim, filled with water
fresh puffed rice (pori, murmura). No pori? Cut a drinking straw into pieces 5 millimetres long
a spoon, a clock and a notebook

activities.record: Count the separate rafts and single grains just after scattering, after 1 minute and after 3 minutes. Write the three numbers. You can also take a photo of the bowl each time.

setup.art: A wide steel bowl of still water with about thirty grains of puffed rice scattered singly across the surface.
setup.caption: 1. Scatter about 30 grains of pori on still water, far apart.

setup.art: The same bowl a minute later, with the grains gathered into four or five rafts and some stuck to the rim.
setup.caption: 2. Do not touch. Watch for 3 minutes and count the rafts.

setup.art: A spoon stirring the bowl gently so that the rafts break up into single grains again.
setup.caption: 3. Stir to break the rafts. Watch again.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl and let the water go still. 2. Ask what the grains will do if nobody touches them, and why. 3. Scatter about 30 grains, as far apart as you can. 4. Count the separate pieces at once.
flow.say: I will scatter these grains on the water and we will not touch them. Will they stay apart, or move? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the grains will do if nobody touches them. Say why. Scatter 30 grains on still water. Count the separate pieces.
flow.parent: Drop the grains from close to the water so they do not sink. Fresh, crisp pori floats best.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pori Rafts. Here you guess what scattered grains will do on still water.

flow.do: 1. Watch without touching the bowl or the table. 2. Count the separate rafts and single grains after 1 minute. 3. Count again after 3 minutes. 4. Your child tells you what they see.
flow.say: Watch two grains that are close together. What happens when they get near each other? How many separate pieces are there now?
flow.kid: Watch without touching. Count the pieces after 1 minute. Count again after 3 minutes. Tell your grown-up what you see.

ask.q: Nobody pushed the grains. So what brought them together?
good: The water pulled them together.
Something about the water surface near each grain.

flow.parent: Each floating grain bends the water surface a little. Two grains close together slide towards each other along that bend. After about 5 minutes the pori gets soggy and may sink, so count before then.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Pori Rafts. Here you watch the grains gather into rafts and count them.

flow.do: 1. Stir gently to break the rafts. 2. Watch them form again. 3. Ask whether the new rafts are the same as before. 4. Read the note for parents aloud and talk about it.
flow.say: The rafts formed again with nobody arranging them. Inside a cell, new virus coat proteins find each other in a similar way. What is the same, and what is different?
flow.kid: Stir to break the rafts. Watch them form again. Are they the same shape as before? Nobody arranged them.
flow.parent: This is a model, so it is not exact. The pori is pulled by the water surface. Virus proteins are pulled by their shapes and electric charges, which fit only one way. That is why pori makes a different raft each time, and virus proteins make the same coat every time. In 1955, Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat and Robley Williams took tobacco mosaic virus apart into protein and RNA in a test tube. When they mixed the two again, whole viruses formed that could infect a leaf.

check.q: New virus coats form inside a cell with no builder to arrange the parts. How?
options: The parts fit together by their shapes and charges
The virus particle pushes each part into place
The cell's nucleus sticks them together by hand
check.why: Coat proteins and the genome join by themselves, because their shapes and electric charges fit. Scientists call this self-assembly. It works even in a test tube. Choosing 'the virus pushes each part' forgets that a virus has no tools or energy of their own.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pori Rafts. Here you break the rafts, watch them form again and link this to a virus's coat.

activities.title: Soap and the Fatty Coat: why soap inactivates some viruses
activities.context: In this activity you shake oil with water in two bottles, one with soap and one without. You see what soap does to a layer of fat. Many viruses, such as flu viruses, are wrapped in a thin layer of fat called an envelope.

materials.item: small clear bottles or jars with tight lids
water
materials.qty: half a glass for each bottle

materials.item: cooking oil
liquid soap or dishwashing liquid
a clock and a notebook

activities.safety: Do not drink from the bottles. Wipe up any spilt oil or soap, because it makes the floor slippery.
activities.record: Draw both bottles just after shaking and again 2 minutes later, or take a photo each time. Label the oil, the water and the cloudy part.

setup.art: Two small clear bottles half full of water, each with a thin golden layer of oil floating on top, labelled A and B.
setup.caption: 1. Half fill two bottles with water. Add 1 teaspoon of oil to each.

setup.art: A hand squeezing five drops of green dishwashing liquid into bottle B only.
setup.caption: 2. Add 5 drops of liquid soap to bottle B only.

setup.art: The two bottles standing after shaking: A with the oil back in a clear layer on top, B evenly milky from top to bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Shake both 20 times. Stand them down and watch for 2 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Half fill both bottles with water. 2. Add 1 teaspoon of oil to each and look at where the oil goes. 3. Add 5 drops of liquid soap to bottle B only. 4. Ask what will be different after shaking, and why.
flow.say: Both bottles have oil and water. Only bottle B has soap. When we shake them and wait, what will be different? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Half fill two bottles with water. Add a teaspoon of oil to each. Add soap to bottle B only. Guess what shaking will do. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soap and the Fatty Coat. Here you set up two bottles of oil and water and guess what soap will change.

flow.do: 1. Close both lids tightly. 2. Shake each bottle 20 times. 3. Stand them side by side. 4. Look at once, after 1 minute and after 2 minutes. 5. Your child points to where the oil is in each bottle and tells you what they see.
flow.say: Watch the oil in bottle A. Where is it going? Now look at bottle B. Can you find the oil at all?
flow.kid: Close the lids. Shake each bottle 20 times. Stand them down. Look now, after 1 minute and after 2 minutes. Point to the oil in each bottle and say what you see.
flow.parent: In bottle A the oil gathers into drops and floats back to the top within a minute or two. Bottle B stays milky, because the soap has broken the oil into drops too small to see and keeps them apart.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Soap and the Fatty Coat. Here you shake both bottles and watch what happens to the oil.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the soap did to the oil. 2. Explain that a soap molecule has one end that holds water and one end that holds fat. 3. Ask what soap might do to a virus wrapped in fat. 4. Read the note together.
flow.say: A soap molecule holds fat at one end and water at the other. A flu virus is wrapped in a thin layer of fat. So what do you think soap does to that virus?
flow.kid: What did the soap do to the oil? A flu virus wears a thin coat of fat. What might soap do to that coat?

ask.q: What do you think soap does to a virus with a fatty envelope?
good: It pulls the fat layer apart, as it broke up the oil.
Without the envelope the virus cannot get into a cell.

flow.parent: Soap pulls the envelope apart. The spikes that fit the cell's receptors sit in the envelope, so the virus can no longer enter a cell. Not every virus has an envelope. Flu, measles and coronaviruses do. Polio, rotavirus and most cold viruses do not, and soap does not break them. Washing still helps against those, because soap and running water lift them off the skin and carry them down the drain.

check.q: Why does soap inactivate a flu virus but not a polio virus?
options: A flu virus has an envelope of fat, and polio has none
A polio virus is too big for soap
Soap works only on plant viruses
check.why: Soap pulls fat apart. A flu virus is wrapped in an envelope of fat, which carries the spikes they need to enter a cell. A polio virus has only a protein coat. Washing still carries polio viruses off the hands, which is why hand washing matters for both.

flow.context: This is the last step of Soap and the Fatty Coat. Here you connect the bottles to a virus's envelope, and learn which viruses have none.

activities.title: A Being for Another World: invent a life form and test it
activities.context: In this activity you invent a living being for a world that is not like Earth. You decide what liquid they live in, where their energy comes from and how their instructions are copied. Then you test your being against NASA's definition of life.

materials.item: plain paper and colour pencils, or clay or kitchen things to build with
a notebook

activities.record: Draw or build your being and label four things: the liquid, the energy supply, the boundary and the instructions. Next to the being, write NASA's three parts and tick the ones your being passes.

setup.art: A notebook page with three world cards drawn on it: an orange moon with dark lakes, a white icy moon with a hidden ocean, and a hot cloudy planet.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a world: Titan's methane lakes, the ocean under Europa's ice, or the clouds of Venus.

setup.art: A child's colourful drawing of a strange flat creature in an orange lake, with four labels: liquid, energy, boundary, instructions.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a being for that world. Label the liquid, the energy, the boundary and the instructions.

setup.art: The same drawing with three boxes underneath marked 'chemical system', 'self-sustaining' and 'can evolve', two ticked and one with a question mark.
setup.caption: 3. Test your being against the three parts of NASA's definition.

flow.do: 1. Read out the three worlds. Titan has lakes of oily liquid methane at 179 degrees below zero. Europa has a dark salty ocean under thick ice. Venus has clouds of acid drops, with mild temperatures high up. 2. Your child chooses one. 3. Ask what any living being would need there.
flow.say: Choose one of these three worlds. Before you draw anything, tell me what a living being would need there. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Choose Titan, Europa or Venus. What would a living being need there? Say why. Do not draw yet.

ask.q: What would any living being need on your world?
good: A liquid, so that chemicals can meet.
A supply of energy, because there may be little sunlight.
A way to pass on instructions.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Being for Another World. Here you choose a world and think about what any life would need there.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws or builds their being. 2. They label the liquid the being lives in. 3. They label where the energy comes from. 4. They label the boundary that keeps the inside in. 5. They label how the instructions are stored and copied.
flow.say: Show me your being, drawn or built. Then show me four things. What liquid are they in? Where does their energy come from? What keeps their inside in? How are their instructions copied?
flow.kid: Draw your being, or build it from clay or things from the kitchen. Label the liquid. Label the energy supply. Label the boundary. Label how the instructions are copied.
flow.parent: There are no wrong beings, but ask for a reason for each label. If your child did Two Liquids, ask what the being's membrane must not dissolve in.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of A Being for Another World. Here you draw your being and label four things about them.

flow.do: 1. Write NASA's three parts next to the being: chemical system, self-sustaining, can evolve. 2. Your child ticks each part the being passes and says why. 3. Ask how a space probe could tell that this being is alive.
flow.say: NASA says life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can evolve, which means their kind can change over generations. Is your being a chemical system? Do they keep themselves going? Can their kind evolve? How would a probe that has never seen them know they are alive?
flow.kid: Write NASA's three parts next to your being. Tick the ones your being passes. How would a space probe know your being is alive?
flow.think: Which part of your being is the same as life on Earth? Could you change that part too?

check.q: Why might a test that looks for DNA fail to find life on another world?
options: Life there might store instructions in another chemical
DNA is too small to find
Other worlds have no chemicals
check.why: DNA is how Earth's life stores instructions, but scientists have built other chemicals, called XNAs, that can do the same job. Life elsewhere might use one of those, or something else. A DNA test would miss it.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Being for Another World. Here you test your invented being against NASA's three parts.

activities.title: Switch Sides: argue that a virus is alive, then that they are not
activities.context: In this activity two people debate whether a virus is alive. After three minutes they swap sides and argue the opposite. It shows that both sides have real evidence.

materials.item: slips of paper for evidence cards
a pen and a clock or timer

activities.record: Write the strongest point you heard for each side. Then write which side you lean towards today, and what would change your mind.

setup.art: Eight paper slips on a table, each with one short fact about viruses written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Write the eight evidence cards and read them together.

setup.art: A girl and her father sitting across a table, each holding four slips, with a timer between them.
setup.caption: 2. One side argues 'alive' and the other 'not alive', for 3 minutes.

setup.art: The same two people having swapped chairs and slips, the girl now pointing at a different slip.
setup.caption: 3. Swap sides and argue the opposite.

flow.do: 1. Write one fact on each slip. Viruses have genes. Viruses evolve. Cells copy them in thousands. Some viruses sense signals and choose a path. A virus particle makes no energy. A virus has no ribosomes. A virus can be stored as crystals. A virus can be built from bottled chemicals. 2. Your child sorts the slips by which side each one helps.
flow.say: Here are eight true facts about viruses. Which ones help the side that says 'alive'? Which help the side that says 'not alive'? Are there any that help both?
flow.kid: Write the eight facts on slips. Sort them. Which help 'alive'? Which help 'not alive'? Do any help both?
flow.context: This is the first step of Switch Sides. Here you write the eight evidence cards and decide which side each one helps.

flow.do: 1. Toss a coin for sides. 2. Each side speaks for 1 minute, then answers the other for half a minute. 3. Swap sides and slips. 4. Repeat, with each person now arguing the opposite.
flow.say: We toss a coin. One of us argues that a virus is alive. The other argues that a virus is not alive. Use at least two evidence cards. Then we swap sides and argue the opposite just as well.
flow.kid: Toss a coin for sides. Speak for 1 minute. Use two evidence cards. Then swap sides. Argue the opposite just as well.
flow.parent: Playing alone, your child argues one side aloud to you, then the other. The swap matters most. It is easy to argue for what you already think.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Switch Sides. Here you debate for three minutes, then swap sides and debate again.

flow.do: 1. Ask which facts the two sides disagreed about. 2. Ask what they did disagree about. 3. Your child writes the strongest point for each side.
flow.say: Did the two sides disagree about any fact?
flow.kid: Think about the facts each side used. Then write the best point for each side.

ask.q: If both sides agree on every fact, what is the argument about?
good: It is about which test for life matters most.
It is about what the word 'alive' should mean.

check.q: Scientists on both sides of the virus debate agree about what viruses do. What do they disagree about?
options: Whether viruses exist
Which test for life matters most
Whether viruses have genes
check.why: Both sides accept the same facts. One side says doing your own chemistry is what counts, and the other says carrying instructions that evolve is what counts. So the disagreement is about the definition, and no new fact about viruses would settle it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Switch Sides. Here you say where the two sides really disagree.

projects.title: The Family Verdict: what do people think 'alive' means?
projects.context: In this project you ask ten people whether a virus is alive, and why. You then sort their reasons, to find out which test for life each person is using without knowing it.

materials.item: a notebook and a pen
a phone, to ring relatives and friends
chart paper or a plain sheet, and colour pencils

schedule.what: Write the three questions, guess the result and try the survey on one person.
Ask nine more people, in person or by phone, and write down each answer and reason.
Tally the answers, sort the reasons, draw a bar chart and write a short report.

projects.record: Keep a table with one row for each person: their name, their answer (alive, not alive or not sure), and their reason in their own words. On day 3, add a bar chart (or a photo of your coin piles) and a report of five sentences.

setup.art: A notebook page with three survey questions written neatly and a blank table with ten rows below.
setup.caption: 1. Write three questions and a table for ten people.

setup.art: A girl on the phone with a notebook on her knee, writing down what her grandfather is saying.
setup.caption: 2. Ask ten people, and write each reason in their own words.

setup.art: A hand-drawn bar chart with three bars labelled 'alive', 'not alive' and 'not sure', and a list of reasons sorted under two headings.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar chart and sort the reasons by the test each person used.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes three questions. Is a virus alive? Why do you think so? Is a dry seed alive? 2. They guess how the ten answers will divide, and why. 3. They try the survey on you and write down your answers.
flow.say: Before you ask anyone, guess the result. Out of ten people, how many will say a virus is alive? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write three questions. Guess how many of ten people will say 'alive'. Say why. Try the survey on one person.
flow.parent: Answer honestly, in your own words. The seed question is there because people who say 'a virus does nothing, so not alive' often still call a dry seed alive.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Family Verdict. Here you write the survey, guess the result and try it on one person.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks nine more people. Aim for different ages. 2. They write each answer as alive, not alive or not sure. 3. They write the reason in the person's own words. 4. They do not tell anyone the 'right' answer.
flow.say: Ask the questions the same way each time. Write down the reason exactly as the person says it. Do not tell them what you think.
flow.kid: Ask nine more people. Ask the same way each time. Write each answer. Write each reason in the person's own words.
flow.parent: Phone calls to grandparents, cousins and neighbours work well. Each call takes about two minutes.
flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of the Family Verdict. Here you ask nine more people and write down their reasons.

flow.do: 1. Your child tallies the three answers and draws a bar chart, or makes a pile of coins for each answer. 2. They sort the reasons into 'what it does', 'what it is made of', 'it evolves or has genes', and 'other'. 3. They count how many people answered differently for the virus and the seed. 4. They write five sentences about what they found.
flow.say: Which kind of reason did people give most? Did anyone say a virus is not alive because they do nothing, and then say a dry seed is alive?
flow.kid: Tally the answers. Draw a bar chart, or stack coins in a pile for each answer. Sort the reasons into kinds. Who answered differently for the seed? Write five sentences.

ask.q: What does it tell you if someone uses one test for the virus and another for the seed?
good: People have more than one idea of 'alive' and switch between them.
The word is not as clear as it seems.

check.q: Ten people are asked if a virus is alive, and they disagree. What is the most likely reason?
options: Some of them know different facts about viruses
They are using different tests for 'alive'
Viruses are alive only on some days
check.why: Most people know roughly the same facts: a virus is tiny, spreads and needs a host. They disagree because one person's test is 'does things by itself' and another's is 'makes more of its kind'. Scientists disagree for the same reason.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Family Verdict. Here you tally the answers, sort the reasons and write the report.

challenges.title: Block the Key: stop a virus entering without harming the cell
challenges.context: This is a design challenge with cardboard. A virus enters a cell because a spike on their coat fits a receptor, as a key fits a lock. You design ways to stop the key fitting, without damaging the lock, because the cell needs the lock for their own work.
challenges.problem: Cut a cardboard 'lock' and a 'key' that fits it. Then find at least two different ways to stop the key going into the lock. The lock must stay whole and uncovered.
constraints: Do not cut, bend or cover the lock. The cell needs their receptor.
Do not throw the key away. Viruses will keep arriving.
Your blocker must not stop the 'friendly key', a second key of a different shape that also uses this lock.
materials: thin cardboard from a cereal or biscuit box
paper, sticky tape and paper clips
general: Make a small paper cap that fits over the tip of the virus key, so that the tip no longer fits the lock. This is how an antibody works.
Stick a blob of tape on the tip of the key.
creative: Cut several loose copies of the lock and scatter them. The keys stick in the loose locks and never reach the cell. Scientists test such 'decoy receptors' as medicines.
Make a cap that fits only the notch pattern on the virus key, so that the friendly key is left alone.
Make a clip that holds two virus keys together, so that neither can turn into the lock.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own blocker. Draw it or just build it, and test it five times. Then ask someone to snip a small piece off the tip of the virus key, so that the key still fits the lock. Does your blocker still fit the key? What would you have to do next?

setup.art: A square of cardboard with a stepped notch cut into one edge, labelled 'cell receptor', and a cardboard strip whose stepped end fits the notch exactly, labelled 'virus key'.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a lock with a stepped notch, and a virus key that fits it.

setup.art: A second cardboard key with a different-shaped tip that also slides into the same notch, labelled 'friendly key'.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a friendly key of a different shape that also fits the lock.

setup.art: A small folded paper cap over the tip of the virus key, which is held near the lock and no longer able to enter.
setup.caption: 3. Design a blocker that stops the virus key and lets the friendly key in.

flow.do: 1. Cut a cardboard square 10 centimetres wide. 2. Cut a stepped notch 2 centimetres deep into one edge. This is the lock. 3. Cut a strip whose end fits the notch exactly. This is the virus key. 4. Cut a second strip with a narrower tip that also slides into the notch. This is the friendly key.
flow.say: The notch is a receptor on a cell. The cell uses it every day. The first strip is a virus's spike. The second is something the cell needs. Both fit.
flow.kid: Cut a cardboard lock with a stepped notch. Cut a virus key that fits it. Cut a friendly key that also fits.
flow.parent: Cardboard from a cereal box cuts easily with ordinary scissors. Help with the notch if the cardboard is thick. Draw a zigzag on the virus key so the two keys are easy to tell apart.
flow.context: This is the first step of Block the Key. Here you cut the lock and the two keys.

flow.do: 1. Read the rules: the lock stays whole and uncovered, and the friendly key must still fit. 2. Your child picks an ordinary idea, such as a paper cap for the key. 3. They say why it should work. 4. They build it and test it five times with both keys.
flow.say: Which idea will you try first? Why should it work? Remember to test the friendly key as well.
flow.kid: Rules: the lock stays whole and uncovered, and the friendly key must still fit. Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Build it. Test both keys five times.

ask.q: Why is it better to block the key than to cover the lock?
good: The cell needs the lock for their own work.
A cap on the key stops only the virus.

flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of Block the Key. Here you try one of the usual solutions and test it.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs and builds a blocker of their own. 2. They test it five times. 3. Now snip a small corner off the key's tip. The key must still enter the lock. 4. Test the blocker on the changed key.
flow.say: Now I am a copying mistake. I change the tip of the key a little, and it still fits the lock. Does your blocker still hold on to it?
flow.kid: Design your own blocker. Build it and test it five times. Now the key's tip is changed. Does your blocker still fit?
flow.parent: A cap made to fit the old tip usually falls off the new one. This is what happens with flu. The virus's spike changes by mutation, last year's antibodies fit less well, and a new vaccine is made.

check.q: A vaccine gives the body antibodies that fit a virus's spike. Why might the same vaccine work less well some years later?
options: The antibodies get tired
Mutations have changed the shape of the spike
The cell's receptor has disappeared
check.why: An antibody fits one exact shape. Copying mistakes change the spike a little, and viruses whose spikes escape the antibodies are copied more. After some years the common spike has a new shape, so the old antibodies fit badly.

flow.context: This is the last step of Block the Key. Here you design your own blocker, and then the virus key changes shape.

challenges.title: The Mistake-Proof Message: design a way to copy without errors
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about copying. In the Copying Chain, copies of copies drifted. Here you copy a message of 24 letters through six copyists, and design a checking system that keeps it free of mistakes. Your cells have such a system. Most RNA viruses, whose instructions are written in the letters A, U, G and C, do not. You will find out how many mistakes slip in, and whether checking is worth the time.
challenges.problem: A message of 24 letters, made only of A, U, G and C, must be copied six times in a chain, each copy made from the last copy. Each copyist may look at the parent for only 5 seconds at a time. Design a system so that copy 6 matches the original exactly.
constraints: Only the first copy may be made from the original. After that, each copy is made from the last copy.
A copyist may look at the parent for 5 seconds, then must cover it before writing. They may look again as many times as they like.
You may add extra marks or extra letters to the message, as long as they are copied too.
materials: a clock or timer with a seconds hand
a book or card to cover the parent message
general: Break the message into groups of three letters with small gaps, so that each look takes in one or two groups.
After writing, compare the copy with the parent letter by letter and correct any mistake. This is proofreading.
creative: Add a check number at the end, such as how many A's the message has. If the count in a copy is wrong, there is a mistake somewhere.
Make two copies each time, compare them with each other, and look again only where they differ.
Give a second person the job of checker, who never copies and only compares.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own copying system. Write its rules in three lines. Run it for six copies and count the wrong letters in copy 6. How many seconds did your system add to each copy? Was it worth it?

setup.art: A paper slip with the 24-letter message AUGGCAUUCGAAGCUUACGGAUCC written in capitals, and a book lying ready to cover it.
setup.caption: 1. Write the message on a slip. Look for 5 seconds, cover it, then write what you remember.

setup.art: Six slips in a row, each a copy of the one before, with two letters circled in red on the last slip where it differs from the first.
setup.caption: 2. First, copy it six times with no system, and count the wrong letters in copy 6.

setup.art: A slip where the same message is written in groups of three letters with a small number at the end, and a second child comparing two slips letter by letter.
setup.caption: 3. Design a checking system, copy six times again, and count the wrong letters.

flow.do: 1. Write the message on a slip. 2. Your child looks at it for 5 seconds, covers it and writes what they remember. They may look again, 5 seconds at a time. 3. They copy that copy, and so on, six times. 4. Compare copy 6 with the original and count the wrong letters.
flow.say: First we need the number to beat. Copy the message six times, each from the last copy, working fast. How many letters are wrong at the end?
flow.kid: Look at the message for 5 seconds. Cover it. Write what you remember. Copy your copy. Do this six times. Count the wrong letters.
flow.parent: Ask your child to work quickly and without checking. Most children get 2 to 6 wrong letters by copy 6. If there are none, ask them to go faster.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mistake-Proof Message. Here you copy the message six times with no system, to get a number to beat.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas: groups of three, and proofreading each copy. 2. Your child picks one and says why it should help. 3. They copy six times again using it. 4. They count the wrong letters and note the extra time.
flow.say: Which idea will you try? Why should it cut the mistakes? Time yourself as well, because checking is not free.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should help. Copy six times with it. Count the wrong letters. Note the time it took.

ask.q: Why does checking each copy stop the mistakes adding up?
good: A mistake is caught before it is copied into the next one.
Each copy starts from a correct parent again.

flow.context: This is step 2 of 3 of the Mistake-Proof Message. Here you try one of the usual checking systems.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs their own system and writes its rules. 2. They run six copies and count the wrong letters. 3. Compare all three runs: mistakes and time. 4. Read the note together and ask whether a virus would want a perfect system.
flow.say: Your cells check their DNA copies and fix nearly every mistake. Most RNA viruses do no checking. Is that only a weakness? What could a virus gain from mistakes?
flow.kid: Design your own system. Write its rules. Run six copies. Count the wrong letters.
flow.parent: Your cells proofread and repair their DNA, so only about one letter in a thousand million ends up wrong. Checking costs time and energy. Most RNA viruses skip it and get about one letter wrong in ten thousand to a hundred thousand. Most of those copies fail. But a few have a change that hides them from the body's defences, and that is how such viruses keep ahead.

check.q: Most RNA viruses make far more copying mistakes than your cells do. What is one result?
options: They evolve faster
They grow larger
They stop being copied
check.why: More mistakes mean more differences between copies, so there is more for selection to work on. That is why flu viruses change from year to year. Many of the mistaken copies fail, but the virus is copied in such huge numbers that some changed copies do well.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Mistake-Proof Message. Here you design your own system, test it, and ask whether copying mistakes are always bad.

worksheets.title: What a virus is, and what NASA means by life

items.p: Which two parts does every virus have?
opts: A genome and a protein coat
items.why: Every virus has a genome of DNA or RNA and a protein coat called a capsid. Some also have an envelope of fat. A nucleus, a membrane and ribosomes are parts of cells.

items.p: True or false: a virus particle has ribosomes of their own.
items.why: False. Ribosomes are the machines that build proteins, and only cells have them. A virus's proteins are built by the host cell's ribosomes.

items.p: A virus can be copied only inside a living ____.
a: cell
host cell
items.why: A virus has instructions but no ribosomes and no supply of energy. Only a living cell can read the instructions and build new viruses.

items.p: Put the steps by which a cell copies a virus in order.
a: The virus's coat fits a receptor and sticks to the cell
The virus or their genome gets inside
The coat comes off and the genome is free
The cell copies the genome and builds virus proteins
New particles put themselves together
The new particles leave the cell
items.why: The order is attach, enter, uncoat, copy and build, assemble, leave. The cell cannot read the genome until the coat is off, and nothing can leave until new particles have formed.
items: The cell copies the genome and builds virus proteins
The new particles leave the cell
The virus's coat fits a receptor and sticks to the cell
The coat comes off and the genome is free
The virus or their genome gets inside

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These five words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: the protein coat of a virus
an outer layer of fat on some viruses
a molecule on a cell that a virus's coat fits

items.p: Why is it safe to eat a tomato from a plant with mosaic virus?
opts: Our cells have no receptor that fits this virus
The virus stays in the roots
Tomato viruses are too large to swallow
items.why: A virus can enter only a cell whose receptor fits their coat. This virus fits tomato cells and does not fit ours. The virus is in the fruit too, so 'stays in the roots' is not the reason.

items.p: Sort these: does only a cell have it, or do a cell and a virus particle both have it?
items.why: A virus particle shares the genome, the proteins and the ability to mutate. What a virus lacks is the machinery: ribosomes, a supply of energy and a membrane that takes in food.
items: a way to get energy from food
a membrane that takes in food

items.p: True or false: antibiotics inactivate cold viruses.
items.why: False. Antibiotics jam parts that bacteria have, such as the bacterial ribosome. A virus particle has no such parts, so antibiotics do nothing to them.

items.p: In the Copying Chain, which lines wandered furthest from 100 millimetres?
items.why: When each line is copied from the last copy, each new mistake is added to all the earlier ones. Copies made from the original start afresh each time, so they stay close.

items.p: In the Copying Chain, mistakes added up from copy to copy. Why did that not happen when you copied the original?
items.a: Each copy of the original starts from the true length, so it carries only one mistake. In the chain, each copy starts from a line that already holds all the earlier mistakes, and adds one more.
items.why: A strong answer says where each copy starts from. A copy of a copy inherits the old mistakes. A copy of the original does not.

items.p: NASA's definition: life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian ____.
a: evolution
items.why: The full definition is 'a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution'. Evolution means the kind can change over generations, through copies that differ a little.

items.p: Which part of NASA's definition does a virus particle fail?
items.why: A virus is chemical and their kind evolves. But a virus particle takes in no energy and builds nothing, so they do not keep themselves going. Choosing 'capable of evolution' forgets that flu viruses change every year.

items.p: On a drawing of a flu virus cut in half, label the genome, the capsid and the envelope.
a: Genome: the coiled strands in the middle
Capsid: the protein coat round the genome
Envelope: the outer layer of fat with spikes
items.why: The genome is innermost, the capsid surrounds it and the envelope is the outside layer. Not all viruses have an envelope, but a flu virus does.
items.art: A round virus particle cut in half, showing coiled strands in the middle, a layer of repeating blocks around them and a soft outer layer with spikes, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Give one reason for calling a virus alive, and one reason against.
items.a: For: a virus carries genes, is copied and evolves. Against: a virus particle makes no energy and builds nothing, and can be copied only by a cell.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real fact on each side. Other good reasons for: some viruses sense signals and choose a path. Against: a virus can be stored as crystals.

items.p: Here are two views about what soap does to a flu virus.

views.says: A virus is alive when inside a cell. So it is fair to say that soap kills them.
A virus particle on your hand does no chemistry. 'Inactivates' is the honest word.

items.ask: Which word would you use, 'kills' or 'inactivates'? Give your reason.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a word and ties it to a test for life, such as 'a particle that does nothing cannot be killed' or 'something that evolves is alive enough to be killed'.
items.why: Both words are used by scientists. The choice shows which test for life the speaker has in mind.

worksheets.title: Evolving, and the cases in between

items.p: Why do most RNA viruses evolve faster than your own cells?
opts: Their copying enzyme does not check for mistakes
items.why: Your cells check and repair their copies. Most RNA viruses bring a copying enzyme that does no checking, so nearly every new copy has a changed letter. More differences give selection more to work on.

items.p: True or false: every mutation harms the virus that carries it.
items.why: False. Most mutations do harm or make no difference, but a few help, for example by hiding the virus from antibodies. Viruses with those few are copied more.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how a new kind of flu virus becomes common.
a: A cell copies a flu genome and gets one letter wrong
The changed letter alters the shape of the spike a little
Old antibodies fit the changed spike badly
The changed virus enters more cells and is copied more
The changed kind becomes the common one
items.why: A copying mistake comes first. It matters only if it changes something, here the spike. Then selection does the rest: the copies that escape the antibodies are copied more.
items: Old antibodies fit the changed spike badly
The changed kind becomes the common one
A cell copies a flu genome and gets one letter wrong
The changed virus enters more cells and is copied more
The changed letter alters the shape of the spike a little

items.p: A virus whose host cells are bacteria is called a ____.
a: bacteriophage
phage
items.why: Bacteriophage means 'bacteria eater'. Phages are the most common viruses on Earth, and nearly all the viruses in sea water are phages.

items.p: A candle flame is chemical and keeps itself going. Why can a flame not evolve?
opts: It has no instructions that are copied with changes
It lasts too short a time
items.why: Evolution needs copies that differ and pass the differences on. A new flame lit from an old one carries nothing over from it. A flame's shape depends only on the wick, the wax and the air now.

items.p: Each of these fails one part of NASA's definition. Sort them by the part they fail.
items.why: Viruses and viroids carry instructions that evolve, but do no chemistry of their own. Flames and red blood cells keep going for a while, but have no genome to pass on with changes.

items.p: Match each thing to what it is.
items.why: These are the things at the edge of life. Each has less than a cell has, and they differ in what they still keep.
pairs: a bare loop of RNA with no coat
a wrongly folded protein that spreads its shape
a virus with hundreds of genes
a virus whose hosts are bacteria
one virus particle outside a cell

items.p: Carsonella has ribosomes but can live only inside insect cells. What does this show about 'self-sustaining'?
opts: It is a matter of degree
Ribosomes are not needed for life
items.why: Carsonella builds their own proteins but takes most other things from the host. So there is no clean split between 'keeps itself going' and 'does not'. Carsonella is still a cell, because they have ribosomes and a membrane.

items.p: True or false: a giant virus with 1,000 genes can build proteins without a cell.
items.why: False. Even mimivirus has no ribosomes. Having many genes does not help if there is no machine to read them.

items.p: Explain why a mule is a problem for NASA's definition of life.
items.a: A mule cannot have young, so one mule cannot evolve. Yet a mule is clearly alive. So 'capable of evolution' must be about a kind of being over generations, and cannot be tested on one body.
items.why: A strong answer says both things: the mule fails if you test one body, and the fix is to apply the definition to kinds. That fix makes the definition hard to use on a single sample.

items.p: In Soap and the Fatty Coat, soap kept oil spread through water. What does soap do to a flu virus?
opts: Pulls apart the envelope of fat
items.why: A soap molecule holds fat at one end and water at the other. It pulls the fat of the envelope apart, and the spikes in the envelope are lost with it. Without spikes the virus cannot enter a cell.

items.p: In Pori Rafts, grains joined with nobody arranging them. How is that like a virus's coat forming? How is it different?
items.a: Alike: the parts come together by themselves, with no builder. Different: pori is pulled by the water surface and makes a different raft each time. Coat proteins fit by shape and charge, and make the same coat every time.
items.why: A strong answer gives one likeness and one difference. The difference matters: a model shows one feature of the real thing and gets others wrong.

items.p: Draw a slope from 'stone' to 'free-living bacterium'. Place a prion, a viroid, a flu virus and Carsonella along the slope.
items.a: From the stone end: prion, viroid, flu virus, Carsonella, then the free-living bacterium.
items.why: A prion has no genome. A viroid has a genome and no coat. A flu virus has a genome and a coat. Carsonella has ribosomes too, but cannot live outside a host. Each one has a little more than the one before.
items.art: A blank slope rising from left to right, with a stone drawn at the bottom end and a rod-shaped bacterium at the top end.

items.p: Here are three views about whether a virus is alive.

views.says: Life means doing your own chemistry. A virus does none, so a virus is a product of cells.
The particle is only the travelling stage. The infected cell is the virus, living.
Stones, viroids, viruses and bacteria lie on a slope. I ask what each can do, and skip the word.

items.ask: Which view sorts the hard cases best, in your opinion? Name one case it sorts oddly.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and names a weak spot. For example, the biochemist's view sorts a dry seed oddly, and the virologist's view makes one cell into two living beings.
items.why: Each view is held by real scientists. Each sorts most cases well and at least one case oddly, which is why the debate continues.

items.p: Three of these can be copied only inside a cell. Which one can live without a host?
items.why: A curd bacterium needs only milk, warmth and time. Flu viruses, viroids and mimiviruses all need a living cell to copy them.

items.p: A protein on a virus's coat fits a ____ on the cell, as a key fits a lock.
a: receptor
items.why: A receptor is a molecule on the cell's surface that has a job for the cell. A virus can enter only if their coat fits that receptor.

worksheets.title: Other worlds, and what a definition is for

items.p: In Two Liquids, salt dissolved in water and not in oil. What would that mean for life in an oily lake?
opts: It would have to stir harder
items.why: Chemicals must be dissolved to meet and react. Salts and sugars do not dissolve in oily liquids. So life there could not be built from the same chemicals as ours.

items.p: Your cells are wrapped in a membrane of fat. Use your Two Liquids results to explain why fat suits the job.
items.a: The inside and the outside of a cell are both watery. In Two Liquids, ghee did not dissolve in water. So a layer of fat stays whole in water, and keeps the cell's salts and sugars in.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result that fat and water do not dissolve each other. A membrane made of something that dissolved in water would fall apart.

items.p: True or false: scientists have built chemicals other than DNA and RNA that can store instructions.
items.why: True. In 2012 a team built six such chemicals, called XNAs, and showed that they can be copied with changes and selected. So DNA and RNA are not the only possible instruction chemicals.

items.p: Why do most scientists think carbon is a likelier frame for life than silicon?
opts: Carbon chains stay whole in water
items.why: Both atoms make four bonds. But long chains of silicon break apart in water, and silicon joined with oxygen becomes rock. Silicon is common, so 'very rare' is not the reason.

items.p: The science that studies whether there is life beyond Earth is called ____.
a: astrobiology
items.why: Astrobiology joins astronomy and biology. It also studies how life began on Earth, because that tells us where else to look.

items.p: Sort these: probably needed by any life, or perhaps only the way Earth's life does it?
items.why: This is the usual view, and it is a guess from one example. A liquid, energy, a boundary and copied instructions seem hard to do without. Which liquid and which instruction chemical may differ.
items: a liquid for chemicals to meet in
a boundary that keeps the inside in

items.p: Viking's fed Mars soil gave off gas. Why do most scientists doubt that it was life?
opts: No carbon molecules were found in the soil
items.why: Life as we know it is built from carbon molecules, and another Viking instrument found none. Mars soil also holds harsh chemicals that can break down the food and give off gas without life.

items.p: A probe cannot wait generations to watch evolution. Suggest one sign of life it could measure in a day. Say why.
items.a: One answer: look for very complicated molecules in large numbers, because only something following instructions makes many identical complicated molecules. Another: gas given off when the sample is fed, with a heated sample as the control.
items.why: A strong answer names a sign and the reason it points to life. It is even better if it says what could give a false alarm.

items.p: Put these in order from the fewest genes to the most.
a: A viroid (none)
A flu virus (about 12)
Carsonella (182)
A mimivirus (about 1,000)
A human (about 20,000)
items.why: The surprise is in the middle. A giant virus has more genes than the smallest bacterium. So the number of genes does not sort viruses from cells.

items.p: About 8 of every 100 letters in your genome came from viruses. What does that show?
opts: Viruses left their genomes in our ancestors
items.why: Some viruses put their genome into the host's genome. When that happened in an egg or sperm cell long ago, the virus's letters were passed down to every descendant.

items.p: True or false: a definition made from one example may describe only that example.
items.why: True. All life on Earth is related, so we have one example. We cannot yet tell which features every kind of life must have.

items.p: In 2002, scientists built polio virus from bottled chemicals. Did they make something alive? Argue your answer.
items.a: Answers vary. One answer: no, because a virus particle is a chemical, and chemists make chemicals. Another: yes, because the built virus is copied by cells and evolves like any other virus.
items.why: A strong answer says which test for life it is using. The same event counts as 'making life' under one definition and not under another.

items.p: Here are two views about defining life.

views.says: My probe launches in three years. I need a rule now, even a rough one, to choose its instruments.
We know one kind of life. Any rule made now is a guess. Better to wait until we find a second kind.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? Can both be right?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer sees that the two want different things. The scientist needs a tool to work with. The philosopher wants the truth about what life is.
items.why: Both can be right. A working definition is a tool for now. Using it does not mean believing that it is final.

items.p: Draw a living being for a world with no liquid water. Label their liquid, energy supply, boundary and instructions.
items.a: Any being with the four labels and a reason for each. For example: a flat being in a methane lake, with energy from chemicals in the lake, a boundary that does not dissolve in methane, and a chain molecule as instructions.
items.why: A strong drawing gives a reason for each label. The boundary must not dissolve in the being's liquid, and the instructions must be something that can be copied.
items.art: A blank page with a horizon line and an empty lake, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Match each world to the liquid found there.
items.why: Only Earth has liquid water lying on its surface. Europa's water is hidden under ice, and the other two liquids are very unlike water.

items.p: Three of these are parts of NASA's definition of life. Which one is not?
items.why: NASA's definition does not mention cells. That was on purpose, because life elsewhere might not be built from cells like ours.

quiz.p: Which of these does a virus particle have?
quiz.why: A virus has a genome and a protein coat. Ribosomes, a nucleus and mitochondria are parts of cells.

quiz.p: Why do antibiotics not work against a cold?
opts: A virus has none of the parts they jam
quiz.why: Antibiotics jam parts that bacteria have, such as their ribosomes and cell walls. A cold is caused by a virus, which has none of these parts.

quiz.p: What must fit together before a virus can enter a cell?
opts: The virus's coat and the cell's receptor
The sizes of the virus and the cell
quiz.why: A protein on the virus's coat must fit a receptor on the cell, as a key fits a lock. That is why each virus has only certain hosts.

quiz.p: What builds the proteins of a new virus?
quiz.why: A virus has no ribosomes. The host cell's ribosomes read the virus's genome and build the virus's proteins. Choosing 'the virus particle' forgets that a particle builds nothing.

quiz.p: Which three things does evolution need?
quiz.why: Evolution happens whenever there are copies, the copies differ a little in ways that are passed on, and some leave more copies than others. Nothing else is needed.

quiz.p: In the Copying Chain, you kept the longest of three copies each time. What happened to the line?
quiz.why: Each copy came out a little long or short by mistake. Keeping the longest each time kept the 'long' mistakes. The line did nothing: copying and choosing did the work.

quiz.p: NASA says life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of what?
quiz.why: The definition ends 'capable of Darwinian evolution'. It means the kind can change over generations through copies that differ.

quiz.p: Which of these passes all three parts of NASA's definition?
quiz.why: A bacterium is chemical, keeps themselves going and evolves. A flame cannot evolve, a virus particle does not sustain themselves, and a crystal does neither.

quiz.p: Scientists who call viruses alive point to which fact?
quiz.why: Viruses carry genes, are copied and evolve. The other three statements are false, and they are the reasons other scientists give for saying viruses are not alive.

quiz.p: Why is NASA's definition called a 'working definition'?
opts: It is useful now and may change
It is used only at work
quiz.why: A working definition is a rule people agree to use for now because it is useful. Scientists expect to change it when they learn more.

quiz.p: Why might life in an oily lake need different chemicals from ours?
opts: Salts and sugars do not dissolve in oil
quiz.why: Chemicals must dissolve in the liquid to meet and react. The salts and sugars our cells use do not dissolve in oily liquids.

quiz.p: In the Two Liquids test, what was the one thing you changed on purpose?
quiz.why: In a fair test you change one thing and keep the rest the same. Here only the liquid changed, so any difference was caused by the liquid.

applications: Vaccines. A vaccine shows the body a weakened virus, an inactivated virus or one virus protein, so the body makes antibodies that fit the real virus's coat.
Medicines against viruses. Since a virus has no chemistry of their own, these medicines block one step of the copying, such as the virus's copying enzyme.
Hand washing. Soap pulls apart the fatty envelope of flu viruses and coronaviruses, and washes other viruses off the skin.
Tracking outbreaks. Scientists read virus genomes from patients and use the mutations to work out how an illness is spreading.
Farming without poison sprays. Indian farmers spray a virus that infects only pod borer caterpillars, and leaves bees, birds and people alone.
Phage therapy. Doctors in Georgia and a few other countries treat some infections with phages, which burst the harmful bacteria. It is being tested more widely.
Planning space missions. A definition of life decides which instruments a probe carries to Mars, Europa or Titan.
Editing genes. CRISPR, the tool scientists use to change genes, was copied from the way bacteria recognise and cut the DNA of phages.

open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree on the facts and disagree on the test. It may never be settled by evidence, because it depends on what we decide the word should mean.
Viruses leave no fossils, and their genomes change too fast to keep old traces. Escaped genes, shrunken cells and a world of viruses before cells are all still possible.

open_questions.q: Is there a second kind of life anywhere, even on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Every living thing found so far shares one ancestor. Our tests look for our own chemistry, so a different kind of life could have been missed.

open_questions.q: Could we recognise life built from other chemicals?
open_questions.why_open: Tests such as counting building steps are new and have been tried on few samples. Nobody has a second kind of life to test them on.

open_questions.q: What is the smallest set of genes that can keep a cell going?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 scientists built a cell with 473 genes, and did not know what about a third of those genes do. Some are still a mystery.

open_questions.q: Does anything like awareness go with the sensing and choosing that viruses and single cells do?
open_questions.why_open: Phages measure a signal and take one of two paths. Whether there is any experience behind that, nobody knows how to test.

ask_kids: Is the cold virus on that door handle alive right now? What about when they are in your nose?
What did you borrow from another living being today?
If you copy a friend's drawing, and she copies yours, and so on, what will the tenth drawing look like?
Why can you catch a cold from your sister but not from the tomato plant?
Is a recipe alive? What does a recipe need before it becomes food?
If we found something on Mars that was copied and evolved but did nothing else, what should we call it?
Which words have no sharp edge, like 'alive'? Is 'tall' one? Is 'evening'?
If soap can break a virus, why do we still need vaccines?

jokes.a: They could not throw one of their own.

jokes.j: Why was the flu virus bad at spelling?
jokes.a: They change a letter every time they are copied.

jokes.j: Why do viruses never pay rent?
jokes.a: They always move in with a host.

jokes.j: What is a virus's favourite game?
What did the soap say to the flu virus?
Why did the scientist take a dictionary to the lab?
jokes.a: To look up 'alive'. It did not help.

jokes.a: At least 123, and every one gives a different answer.
