maths.problem: In Walk the Scale, everything is 10,000 times its real size, so 1 millimetre stands for 100 nanometres. A tobacco mosaic virus is 300 nanometres long. A mimivirus is 700 nanometres across. How big is each in the model?
maths.answer: The tobacco mosaic virus is 3 millimetres long. The mimivirus is 7 millimetres across.
maths.explain: Every 100 nanometres becomes 1 millimetre. 300 ÷ 100 = 3, so the rod is 3 millimetres long. 700 ÷ 100 = 7, so the mimivirus is 7 millimetres across. A flu virus is a 1 millimetre dot, so the mimivirus is 7 times as wide.
maths.context: This is about Walk the Scale, where you made paper models of a virus, a bacterium and a cell at 10,000 times their real size.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can picture a nanometre. Multiplying every size by the same number turns sizes we cannot see into sizes we can hold and compare.

maths.problem: In a made-up Copying Chain, the lines of chain A measured 104, 97, 103, 110, 108, 115, 112, 119, 123 and 121 millimetres. The lines of set B measured 103, 96, 101, 105, 98, 102, 94, 100, 104 and 99. For each, find the biggest gap from 100. How many times as big is chain A's gap?
maths.answer: Chain A's biggest gap is 23 millimetres. Set B's is 6 millimetres. Chain A's gap is nearly 4 times as big.
maths.explain: In chain A the line furthest from 100 is 123, and 123 − 100 = 23. In set B the furthest is 94, and 100 − 94 = 6. 23 ÷ 6 is a little less than 4. Chain A wandered further because each copy passed its mistake on to the next.
maths.context: This is about the Copying Chain, where you copied a 100 millimetre line by eye. Chain A copied the last copy each time. Set B copied the original each time.
maths.why_maths: A list of twenty numbers is hard to compare by looking. The biggest gap from 100 turns each list into one number that shows how far it wandered.

maths.problem: In part 2 of a made-up Copying Chain, the kept lines measured 100, 106, 111, 118, 123 and 130 millimetres for generations 0 to 5. About how much did the line gain each generation? Predict the length at generation 10.
maths.answer: About 6 millimetres each generation. At generation 10 the line should be about 160 millimetres.
maths.explain: From 100 to 130 is a gain of 30 millimetres in 5 generations. 30 ÷ 5 = 6 millimetres each generation. Five more generations add about 5 × 6 = 30. 130 + 30 = 160. Real results will be close to this, not exact.
maths.context: This is about part 2 of the Copying Chain, where you drew three copies each time and kept only the longest.

chart.title: Made-up example: keeping the longest of three

maths.why_maths: Without choosing, the line wanders up and down. With choosing, the gains follow a steady pattern, and a pattern lets you predict generations you have not drawn.

maths.problem: One phage enters a bacterium. Thirty minutes later, 100 new phages burst out, and each enters a new bacterium. How many phages are there after 30, 60 and 90 minutes? Why can this not go on for long?
maths.answer: 100 after 30 minutes, 10,000 after 60 minutes and 1,000,000 after 90 minutes. It stops when the phages run out of bacteria.
maths.explain: Each round multiplies the number by 100. 1 × 100 = 100. 100 × 100 = 10,000. 10,000 × 100 = 1,000,000. One more round would need a million bacteria. Soon there are too few hosts, and the numbers fall.
maths.context: This is about how a cell copies a virus. A phage is a virus whose hosts are bacteria, such as the T4 phage in the game Who Fits Whom?
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by 100 again and again grows far faster than people expect. It explains how one virus particle can become an illness in a few days.

maths.problem: A flu virus genome has about 13,500 letters. Suppose the copying gets 1 letter wrong in every 10,000, which is a round figure. One infected cell makes 1,000 copies. About how many wrong letters are there in all those copies together?
maths.answer: About 1,350 wrong letters, which is one or two in each copy.
maths.explain: 1,000 copies of 13,500 letters is 13,500,000 letters. One in every 10,000 is wrong. 13,500,000 ÷ 10,000 = 1,350. Shared among 1,000 copies, that is between one and two wrong letters in each copy. So nearly every new flu virus differs a little from the parent.
maths.context: This is about copying mistakes. In the Mistake-Proof Message you counted wrong letters after six copies. Here the copyist is a cell copying a flu virus.
maths.why_maths: A rate such as 'one in ten thousand' sounds tiny. Multiplying it by the number of letters copied shows that mistakes are certain, and common.

maths.problem: Your genome has about 3,000 million letters. About 8 percent came from viruses. The parts that hold instructions for proteins make up about 1.5 percent. How many letters is each? How many times as large is the virus share?
maths.answer: 240 million letters came from viruses. 45 million letters hold protein instructions. The virus share is more than 5 times as large.
maths.explain: 1 percent of 3,000 million is 30 million. 8 percent is 8 × 30 = 240 million. 1.5 percent is 30 + 15 = 45 million. 240 ÷ 45 is a little more than 5.
maths.context: This is about the old virus genomes in human DNA. Viruses that infected our ancestors left their letters in the genome that was passed down to us.
maths.why_maths: Percentages let you compare two parts of a very large whole. Here they show that more of your genome came from viruses than is used for your own protein instructions.

playtest: Every part was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so please treat amounts and times as a starting point. The Copying Chain (the main investigation) needs only paper, a pencil and a ruler. Its result depends on the copier: chain A usually wanders 15 to 40 millimetres from 100, but a chain can wander away and come back, so the step says to look at the furthest point or to draw a second chain. The copier must turn the parent line face down before drawing, or the copies come out too exact to show anything. Do not measure until all the drawing is done. In part 2 the child must still try to copy exactly. Two Liquids uses about half a cup of cooking oil, which can be strained and cooked with the same day. Turmeric is the hard result: some powder settles in both liquids, so compare the liquid above the powder, which is clear yellow in oil and cloudy in water. In a cold room ghee mixes into oil slowly, so that glass gets ten minutes. Live, Killed or Inactivated? works without a vaccination card, using the list in step 1. Pori Rafts needs fresh, crisp pori, which gets soggy after about five minutes. Soap and the Fatty Coat needs bottles with tight lids. Block the Key needs a grown-up for cutting thick cardboard. In the Mistake-Proof Message, a careful child may make no mistakes in the first run, and the step says to speed up. The Family Verdict needs ten people, and phone calls count. Nothing needs a garden. Facts were checked from memory against the papers listed in the sources, with no library to hand. Figures a person may wish to check: about ten million viruses in a millilitre of sea water, a fifth of the sea's microbes killed by viruses each day, 8 percent of the human genome from viruses, 182 genes in Carsonella, about 1,000 genes in mimivirus, and the Dragonfly dates of 2028 and 2034. The mistake rates for copying are round figures. The three video addresses were confirmed, but the films were not watched.
